Collision-free Movement on Grids and Beyond

Hendrik Molter    Meirav Zehavi
Abstract

We study collision-free movement problems on graphs, where the task is to coordinate a set of robots so that they reach a target formation satisfying a desired property while minimizing the total travel distance. This framework extends two classical models: (a) minimizing movement [Demaine et al., TALG ’09, ’14], which does not enforce collision avoidance, and (b) coordinated motion planning or multi-agent path finding [Eiben et al., SoCG ’23, Deligkas et al., ICALP ’24, among many others], where each robot is assigned an explicit target position.

We focus on the setting where the target formation of the robots should be connected. We analyze the parameterized complexity of the problem with respect to the number of (main) robots and the total travel length on grid graphs and two natural generalizations thereof: planar graphs and unit disk graphs.

1 Introduction

Coordinated motion of robots is a fundamental task in computational geometry and robotics. The environment is frequently modeled by a grid, often consisting also of “obnoxious robots” in addition to the “main robots”. Within the environment, the main robots are set to move so as to perform a predetermined task; the obnoxious robots, on the other hand, are simply meant to model movable obstacles. To date, most efforts were directed at the following:

  1. 1.

    Given a target position for each main robot, plan a collision-free motion for all robots so that each main robot will reach its target (see, e.g., [10, 16, 41, 42, 21, 36, 39]). This setting, widely known as MAPF (Multi-Agent Path Finding), was part of the 3rd Computational Geometry Challenge of SoCG 2021 [18].

  2. 2.

    Given a formation for all main robots (where a formation of particular interest is to induce a connected set), plan a motion (collisions allowed) of all robots as to achieve this formation (see, e.g., [12, 11, 3, 26]).

Both objectives have been extensively studied in a variety of discrete and continuous settings, from both a theoretical perspective—particularly in the frameworks of parameterized complexity [10, 16, 12, 21, 17] and approximation algorithms [11, 3, 36]—and a practical perspective [18, 40]. The above leaves open a very obvious and natural question:

What about the task of, given a characterization of a formation for all main robots, planning a collision-free motion of all robots as to achieve this formation?

To the best of our knowledge, the present work is the first to address this problem. As in the classical settings discussed above, two natural optimization goals arise: (i) minimize the total number of moves taken by all robots, i.e.,the total energy; (ii) minimize the number of time steps needed, i.e., the makespan. Here, we focus on the first goal, while the desired formation is to establish a connected set. We provide a spectrum of parameterized results for grids and generalizations thereof, with respect to the two most natural parameters in this context: the number of main robots (kk), and the total energy to spend (cc). Notably, our results delineate the subtle boundaries between various tractable and intractable cases.

Previous works most closely related to ours—i.e., which focus on parameterized complexity, environments modeled by graphs (particularly grids), and total energy minimization, are Eiben et al. [16] and Deligkas et al. [10] for the first task, and Demaine et al. [12] for the second task. Discussion (non-exhaustive) of some other related works can be found at the end of this section.

Eiben et al. [16] studied MAPF on solid grids with both (total) energy and makespan minimization as objectives, and without obnoxious robots. This generalizes the well-known (n2−1)(n^{2}-1)-Puzzle, which was extensively studied before and is known to be NP-hard [38, 13]. They showed (for solid grids only) that both energy and makespan minimization problems are fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) w.r.t. the number of (main) robots kk, the energy minimization problem is FPT w.r.t. the energy cc, and the makespan minimization problem is paraNP-hard w.r.t. the makespan. The follow-up work by Deligkas et al. [10] focused on (total) energy minimization, in the presence of obnoxious robots (thereby closely related to the Rush Hour problem, which was also extensively studied before [22, 20]). Further, they considered general graphs, and showed: FPT w.r.t. the number of obnoxious robots ℓ\ell when k=1k=1; FPT w.r.t. the total number of robots k+ℓk+\ell plus the treewidth of the input graph; FPT approximation w.r.t. k+ℓk+\ell and additive error; W[1]-hardness w.r.t. cc; FPT w.r.t. cc on planar graphs. In further follow-up, Deligkas et al. [9] show that the problem is W[1]-hard w.r.t. cc even if k=1k=1 and FPT w.r.t. kk plus the treedepth of the input graph. It remains open whether the problem is FPT w.r.t. k+ℓk+\ell.

Demaine et al. [12] studied the parameterized complexity of a very general problem addressing movement to specific formations and for several objectives, including both main and obnoxious robots. Here, recall, collisions are allowed (also in the final formation itself). They provided a dichotomy that asserted that, when the family of possible formations, ℱ\cal F, is decidable and closed under edge-addition, the problem is FPT w.r.t. kk if the edge-minimal formations in ℱ\cal F have bounded treewidth, and W[1]-hard otherwise. In particular, this asserts that the problem where we aim to move robots so that the main robots will form a connected set, and with the objective of energy minimization, is FPT w.r.t. kk. We remark that this case (of connectivity) has received previous focused attention, particularly from the viewpoint of approximation (see, e.g., [3]). Additionally, Demaine et al. [12] provided W[1]-hardness w.r.t. kk for the setting where the formation is a hereditary property that does not contain all cliques or all independent sets.

1.1 Our Contributions

We refer to the problem introduced here as Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. If results hold for more general formations we call the problem Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. All formal definitions are given in Section 3. Recall that kk is the number of main robots, ℓ\ell is the number of obnoxious robots, and cc is the (total) energy bound. We start by discussing some results that are easy to obtain or follow straightforwardly from the literature [11, 12] in Section 3. Notably, we have the following.

  • •

    If ℓ=0\ell=0, then Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by kk.

  • •

    If Π\Pi is hereditary and does not contain all complete graphs and all empty graphs, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c even if ℓ=0\ell=0.

  • •

    Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard even if ℓ=0\ell=0 and the input graph is planar.

  • •

    If deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi is polynomial-time solvable, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is in XP when parameterized by cc.

In the following, we give a brief description of each of our results and point to the sections where we present the full proofs. In Section 2 we give a more detailed overview on our results and explain the techniques we use to obtain them (deferring the proofs to the later sections).

Note that since connectivity is not hereditary, the W[1]-hardness result for parameter k+ck+c mentioned above does not apply to Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. In Section 4, show the following as our first hardness result.

Theorem 1.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c.

It follows that if we wish to obtain fixed-parameter tractability results for kk, cc, or k+ck+c, we have to restrict the class of input graphs. We focus our investigation on grid graphs, and two natural generalizations: planar graphs and unit disk graphs.

Our main technical hardness result for grids is the following (Section 4).

Theorem 2.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard even if k=2k=2 and the input graph is a grid.

That is, it is hard for just two robots to meet on a grid! We remark that in both hardness results, the instances produced by the reductions have an unbounded number of obnoxious robots, which is not completely unexpected since Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by kk if there are no obnoxious robots.

On the positive side, we provide the following kernelization results in Section 5.

Theorem 3.

Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi parameterized by k+ck+c admits a polynomial kernel of size O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) if the input graph is a grid.

For the case where Π\Pi is connectivity, we can give a better bound on the kernel size.

Theorem 4.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by k+ck+c admits a polynomial kernel of size O⁡(min⁡{k⋅c2,k2+c2})O(\min\{k\cdot c^{2},k^{2}+c^{2}\}) if the input graph is a grid.

Furthermore, we give a number of kernelization lower bounds in Section 5. The constructions used are all based on ideas from the reduction behind Theorem 2. We first show that we presumably cannot obtain polynomial kernels for the parameter k+ck+c on planar graphs. Hence, exploiting the properties of grids is essential for the kernelization algorithms.

Theorem 5.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by cc does not admit a polynomial kernel unless coNP ⊆\subseteq NP/poly, even if the input graph is planar and k=2k=2.

Further, we show that the dependency of the polynomial kernel size on kk for grids presumably is unavoidable.

Theorem 6.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by cc does not admit a polynomial kernel unless coNP ⊆\subseteq NP/poly, even if the input graph is a grid.

Finally, we show that we presumably cannot significantly improve the kernel size given in Theorem 4.

Theorem 7.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by k+ck+c does not admit a polynomial kernel of size O⁡((k+c)2−ε)O((k+c)^{2-\varepsilon}) for any ε>0\varepsilon>0 unless coNP ⊆\subseteq NP/poly, even if the input graph is a grid.

In Section 6, we turn our attention to planar graphs and show the following result.

Theorem 8.

Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k+ck+c if the input graph is planar.

We obtain this result by providing a monadic second-order logic (MSO) formulation of the problem and then employing Courcelle’s famous theorem [2, 5, 6].

In Section 7, we show that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity on unit disk graphs admits an FPT approximation algorithm when parameterized by k+ck+c for the canonical optimization variant of the problem where we aim to minimize the energy.

Theorem 9.

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity admits a fixed-parameter approximation when parameterized by k+ck+c if the input graph is a unit disk graph, that produces a solution with energy at most 2⋅OPT+3​k2\cdot\text{OPT}+3k, where OPT is the energy of an optimal solution.

Finally, we give some open questions and future research directions in Section 8.

1.2 Further Related Work

In recent years there has been intensive research on multi-agent path finding (MAPF) problems in multiple variations [41, 42, 39]. As mentioned, MAPF can be seen as a generalization of the (n2−1)(n^{2}-1)-Puzzle and other so-called pebble motion problems on graphs [28, 43, 38, 13]. It is also closely related to the problem such as Rush Hour [22, 20], Temporally Disjoint Paths [35, 34], the Snake Game [29], and Chip Reconfiguration [7]. To the best of our knowledge, the current state-of-the-art (optimal) algorithms for MAPF problems employ the so-called conflict-based search approach [40].

The following works are more closely related to our problem. Papadimitriou et al. [36] study coordinated motion planning there is only one main robot and show that the problem is NP-hard on planar graphs. They give some further approximation results. Fioravantes et al. [21] study coordinated motion planning where the goal is to minimize the makespan rather than the total energy. They obtain an extensive number of parameterized complexity results. Eiben et al. [17] investigate the parameterized complexity a problem variant, where robots may move an arbitrary distance in each step and the number of step shall be minimized. There is also work on the parameterized complexity of coordinated motion planning problems where the robots have geometric shapes [31, 1].

Various version of the movement problem (where collisions do not matter) have been studied by Demaine et al. [11] from an approximation perspective. Improved approximation results have been given by Berman et al. [3]. Friggstad and Salavatipour [26] study a closely related problem: Mobile Facility Location. Here, facilities and clients should be moved in a graph such that every client is close to a facility. They study approximability of this problem.

2 Overview of Results and Techniques

In this section, we present a more detailed overview on our results, together with intuitive and informal explanations and descriptions of the techniques that we use. Full details and formal proofs can be found in the later sections.

Hardness Resuls (Section 4).

We first show that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c (Theorem 1). To this end, we present a parameterized reduction from Multicolored Clique [19]. Here, given an ℓ\ell-partite graph, we are asked whether it contains a clique of size ℓ\ell. The parameter is ℓ\ell. The reduction uses an edge-selection gadget for every color-combination. Each one has two main robots and one obnoxious robot for each edge. One of the obnoxious robots may be moved (the corresponding edge is “selected”) which enables the two main robots to move to verification gadgets for the colors in the color-combination. Each verification gadget of a color contains “immovable” formations of main robots which can only be connected if the selected edges of the color-combinations containing the color have the same endpoints. For an illustration see Figure 1.

Our main hardness result is that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard on a grid even if there are only two main robots (Theorem 2). We obtain the result via a reduction from Linked Planar 3-SAT [37]. This reduction is described in two construction steps: We first construct a planar instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity and then show how the produced graph can be embedded into a grid (with appropriate modifications). In Linked Planar 3-SAT, we are given a Boolean formula ϕ\phi in 3-CNF with clause set YY and variable set XX, and a graph H=(Y∪X,F)H=(Y\cup X,F) such that the following holds:

  • •

    Graph HH is the union of a Hamiltonian cycle that first visits all elements of XX and then all elements of YY, and the incidence graph of ϕ\phi.

  • •

    Graph HH is planar and there is an embedding where each edge between a clause and a variable that appears negated in the clause is inside the cycle, and each edge between a clause and a variable that appears non-negated in the clause is outside of the cycle.

  • •

    Each variable appears in at most three clauses.

We may assume that we know the embedding of HH and the Hamiltonian cycle [37].

Informally speaking, the main idea on how to reduce from Linked Planar 3-SAT to Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity planar graphs is as follows. We split the Hamiltonian cycle in HH between the last clause vertex and the first variable vertex, in that way obtaining a Hamiltonian path that first traverses all variable vertices and then all clause vertices. If we draw this path horizontally (from left to right), then (in a planar drawing) each edge between a clause and a variable that appears negated in the clause is below the path, and each edge between a clause and a variable that appears non-negated in the clause is above of the path. We add an extra vertex to the beginning of the path and an extra vertex to the end, and place a main robot on each of them. Now we “replace” each variable vertex with the variable gadget illustrated in Figure 2. We connect edges above the path to the three vertices on top of the gadget, and edge below the path to the three vertices below. For an illustration see Figure 3. Then these edges (that originally connected the clause and variable vertices) are subdivided a number of times and obnoxious robots are places on all newly created vertices. Furthermore, obnoxious robots are places on all clause vertices. The idea is that the three obnoxious robots in each variable gadget (see Figure 2) need to move either to the three upper or lower vertices, which will encode setting the variable to true or false. Now the main robot on the left can freely move until the last variable gadget. Then the obnoxious robot on each clause vertex needs to move out of the way. To this end, all obnoxious robots on one of the paths connecting the clause vertex to a variable gadget need to move. This is only possible if the vertex of the variable gadget where the path arrives is free, hence encoding that the corresponding literal satisfies the clause. Now the main robots can freely meet on some adjacent clause vertices.

Afterwards, we modify the informally described graph (call it GG) depicted in Figure 3 to produce a graph G′G^{\prime} that is a grid (together with an embedding that shows this). Note that there are three main obstacles to overcome:

  • •

    The clause vertices in GG may have degree 5, which is not possible in a grid. Hence, we have to modify the vertices to “clause gadgets” that are grids.

  • •

    All paths connecting clause gadgets to variable gadgets need to have the same length in order for the reduction to work.

  • •

    The path between the last variable gadget and the first clause gadget has to be sufficiently long (that is, longer than any path from a clause gadget to a variable gadget) for the reduction to work.

We introduce clause gadgets, which are, informally speaking, small tree-like grids rooted at the clause vertices and three leaves pointing upward, and three pointing downward. All vertices in the gadgets have obnoxious robots, and the paths to the variable gadgets now start at the leaves. In order to ensure that all paths between variable and clause gadgets have the appropriate length, we introduce a “zone” in the grid between all variable gadgets and all clause gadgets, which is sufficiently large such that we can change the length of each path to the desired length by using “snake-like” embeddings in the grid. For an illustration see Figure 4.

Collision Free Movement on Grids (Section 5).

We give several kernelization algorithms and kernelization lower bounds for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity on grids. In fact, our first kernelization algorithm works for general formations Π\Pi. The main insight here is that vertices that are far away from each of the main robots (regardless of whether they are occupied by obnoxious robots or not) cannot be relevant for any solution. This allows us to obtain a reduction rule that, when applied exhaustively, yields a kernel of size O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) for Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi (Theorem 3). If Π\Pi is connectivity, we can improve the size of the kernel. In this case, informally speaking, we have that if a vertex is too far away from some main robot, it cannot be relevant, since eventually, all main robots have to be close together. This allows us to obtain an additional reduction rule. Exhaustively applying both rules yields a kernel of size O⁡(min⁡{k⋅c2,k2+c2})O(\min\{k\cdot c^{2},k^{2}+c^{2}\}) for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity (Theorem 4).

Furthermore, we give a number of kernelization lower bounds, using the well-known framework of OR-cross-compositions [4, 25]. For all results, we cross-compose from Linked Planar 3-SAT and reuse (modified versions of) the constructions devised to obtain Theorem 2. We first show that we presumably cannot obtain polynomial kernels for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by cc on planar graphs, even if k=2k=2 (Theorem 5). To this end, we use the planar instances of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity produced by the reduction behind Theorem 2 before the modifications to obtain a grid are applied (Figure 3). We remove the main robots from each instance, and connect the (previous) starting locations of the main robots to a new starting location with sufficiently long paths (ensuring that the main robots cannot move between instances). For an illustration see Figure 5. This result shows that the restriction to grids is essential for obtaining polynomial kernels.

We further show that we cannot obtain polynomial kernels for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity on grids for the single parameter cc (Theorem 7). Note that Theorem 2 obviously rules out polynomial kernels for the single parameter kk. Here, we use the grid instances produced by the reduction behind Theorem 2. Note that we cannot connect the instances in the same fashion as in the previous cross-composition, as this introduces a high-degree vertex which is not embeddable in a grid. We replace this with a tree-like grid that has a main robots each vertex. Intuitively, we cannot use a single main robot since the distance between its starting location and the instances would be too large. Now, instead of single main robots moving through one of the instances, a “snake” of main robots moves through it to establish a connection between the right and the left side of the instance. To accommodate this, we have to also make some modifications to instances produced by the reduction behind Theorem 2.

Finally, we show that we presumably cannot significantly improve the size of the kernel produced by Theorem 4 (Theorem 7). Here, we use the weak cross-compositions framework [30, 25]. Informally speaking, we have to ensure here that the parameter of the instance produced by the weak cross-composition can be upper-bounded by the maximum size among the input instances multiplied by the square root of the number of input instances. We can achieve this by again using the instances produced by the reduction behind Theorem 2 and arranging the input instances in a grid-like fashion, see Figure 6. Furthermore, we remove the main robots from each input instance and use one main robot starting in the lower left of the arrangement and one in the upper right. Together with appropriate connections between the instances, this ensures that the sum of the distances of both main robots to any of the instances is in O⁡(t⋅xmax)O(\sqrt{t}\cdot x_{\max}), where tt is the number of input instances and xmaxx_{\max} is the maximum instance size.

Collision Free Movement on Planar Graphs (Section 6).

We show that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k+ck+c if the input graph is planar (Theorem 8). Note that this result holds for general formation Π\Pi. We obtain it by providing a monadic second-order logic (MSO) formulation of the problem and then employing Courcelle’s famous theorem [2, 5, 6], stating that MSO Model Checking is fixed-parameter tractable w.r.t the size of the formula and the treewidth of the relational structure on which the formula is defined.

As the relational structure, we take the input graph together with “time steps” that model at which point in a movement a vertex is visited by a robot or an edge is traversed by a robot. Since the number of moves is upper-bounded by cc, we need cc of such time steps. Informally speaking, we associate each time step with each of the vertices and edges, which increases the treewidth of the graph by some factor depending on cc. Additionally, we can remove vertices that are far away from any main robot (similar to the reduction rule in the kernelization algorithm). This allows us to upper-bound the diameter of the input graph by a function in k+ck+c and, since it is planar, also its treewidth. It follows that the treewidth of the relational structure can be upper-bounded by a function in k+ck+c.

Now we define movements as sets of vertex-time step pairs with the following properties:

  • •

    For each time step, there is one vertex-time step pair in the set.

  • •

    For each pair of consecutive time steps, the corresponding vertices are either equal (the robot does not move) or connected by an edge.

  • •

    The vertex corresponding to the first time step is the starting location of a robot.

These properties can be checked with MSO formulas. Furthermore, we can check (with an MSO formula) for each pair of movements, whether the two corresponding robots do not collide. If during a movement, a robot visits a vertex that is the starting location of another robot, there must be another movement moving that robot out of the way. Finally, we can have at most cc non-trivial movements (that is, the robot actually moves at least once). Putting this together, we can obtain an MSO formula that checks for a set of cc movements, whether they are collision-free and also do not collide with any robot that is not moved. Finally, we can straightforwardly determine the locations of all main robots after the movements and check whether the formation has property Π\Pi. We remark that the size of the overall MSO formula only depends on cc and the size of a subformula that checks whether a graph on kk vertices has property Π\Pi (which, notably, is constant if Π\Pi is connectivity).

Collision Free Movement on Unit Disk Graphs (Section 7).

We show that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity on unit disk graphs admits an FPT approximation algorithm when parameterized by k+ck+c for the canonical optimization variant of the problem, where we aim to minimize the energy. More specifically, we give a fixed-parameter approximation for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity on unit disk graphs when parameterized by k+ck+c, that produces a solution with energy at most 2⋅OPT+3​k2\cdot\text{OPT}+3k, where OPT is the energy of an optimal solution (Theorem 9). The algorithm makes use of the fact that unit disk graphs are a subclass of so-called clique grids. Informally speaking, a clique grid, each vertex is associated with a grid cell, and all vertices in the same cell form a clique. All additional edges are between vertices in grid cells of distance at most two.

We start by “guessing” the optimal value for cc, and removing all vertices that are too far away from any main robot starting location (as in the kernelization algorithms). Afterwards, the number of cliques / grid cells in the clique grid is upper-bounded by some function in k+ck+c. Furthermore, we guess a spanning tree that witnesses the connectivity of the formation of the main robots after the movements.

We introduce a type for each vertex of a clique that, intuitively, describes via which cliques the vertex can be reached from each main robot and whether it is occupied by an obnoxious robot. We show how to upper-bound the number of types in a function of cc and kk. We guess the type of each vertex in the spanning tree. Now, informally speaking, we guess up to cc movement vectors of types that move the main robots to vertices of the correct type (as specified by the guesses for the spanning tree), and check whether they are collision-free. When two robots move to vertices of the same type, we need to ensure that these are different vertices to be collision-free. This, intuitively, is where the factor two in the approximation comes from. We potentially need to move robots to a “free” vertex of a certain type, which requires at most one extra move as all vertices of the same type form a clique. Finally, at the end we may need to move all main robots to the “correct” vertex of the guessed type in order to obtain the guessed spanning tree, which, as we show, requires at most three extra moves per main robot.

3 Preliminaries and Known Results

In this section, we provide all necessary notation and terminology, as well as some preliminary results that are easy to obtain or straightforwardly follow from known results.

Parameterized Complexity.

We use the following standard concepts from parameterized complexity theory [8, 15, 23, 25]. A parameterized problem L⊆Σ∗×ℕL\subseteq\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N} is a subset of all instances (x,k)(x,k) from Σ∗×ℕ\Sigma^{*}\times\mathbb{N}, where kk denotes the parameter. A parameterized problem LL is in the class FPT (or fixed-parameter tractable) if there is an algorithm that decides every instance (x,k)(x,k) for LL in f⁡(k)⋅|x|O⁡(1)f(k)\cdot|x|^{O(1)} time for some computable function ff that depends only on the parameter. A decidable parameterized problem LL admits a kernel if there is a polynomial-time algorithm that transforms each instance (x,k)∈{0,1}×ℕ(x,k)\in\{0,1\}\times\mathbb{N} into an instance (x′,k′)∈{0,1}×ℕ(x^{\prime},k^{\prime})\in\{0,1\}\times\mathbb{N} such that |x′|+k′≤f⁡(k)|x^{\prime}|+k^{\prime}\leq f(k), for some computable function ff, and (x′,k′)∈L(x^{\prime},k^{\prime})\in L if and only if (x,k)∈L(x,k)\in L. It is known that a decidable parameterized problem LL admits a kernel if and only if it is fixed-parameter tractable [25]. If ff is a polynomial, that is, |x′|+k′∈rO⁡(1)|x^{\prime}|+k^{\prime}\in r^{O(1)}, we say that LL admits a polynomial kernel. Presumably, not all problems that are fixed-parameter tractable admit a polynomial kernel [25]. We give more details on how to exclude polynomial kernels under standard complexity assumptions in the respective section of the paper. A parameterized problem LL is in the class XP, if there is an algorithm that decides every instance (x,k)(x,k) for LL in |x|f⁡(k)|x|^{f(k)} time for some computable function ff that depends only on the parameter. If a parameterized problem LL is W[1]-hard, then it is presumably not contained in FPT [8, 15, 23].

Graph Theory.

We use standard notation and terminology from graph theory [14]. Let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) with E⊆(V2)E\subseteq\binom{V}{2} be a graph. We denote by V⁡(G)=VV(G)=V and E⁡(G)=EE(G)=E the sets of its vertices and edges, respectively. We use nn to denote the number of vertices of GG. We call two vertices u,v∈Vu,v\in V adjacent if {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E. The degree of a vertex v∈Vv\in V is deg⁡(v)=|{u∣{u,v}∈E}|\deg(v)=|\{u\mid\{u,v\}\in E\}|. We say that a graph G′G^{\prime} is a subgraph of GG if V⁡(G′)⊆V⁡(G)V(G^{\prime})\subseteq V(G) and E⁡(G′)⊆E⁡(G)E(G^{\prime})\subseteq E(G). For some vertex set V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V, we denote by G⁡[V′]G[V^{\prime}] the induced subgraph of GG on the vertex set V′V^{\prime}, that is, G⁡[V′]=(V′,E′)G[V^{\prime}]=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}) where E′={{v,w}∣{v,w}∈E∧v∈V′∧w∈V′}E^{\prime}=\{\{v,w\}\mid\{v,w\}\in E\wedge v\in V^{\prime}\wedge w\in V^{\prime}\}. We further denote G−V′=G⁡[V∖V′]G-V^{\prime}=G[V\setminus V^{\prime}]. We say that a sequence P=({vi−1,vi})i=1ℓP=(\{v_{i-1},v_{i}\})_{i=1}^{\ell} of edges in EE forms a path of length ℓ\ell in GG from v0v_{0} to vℓv_{\ell} if vi≠vjv_{i}\neq v_{j} for all 0≤i<j≤ℓ0\leq i<j\leq\ell. We say that vertices uu and vv are connected in GG if there is a path from uu to vv in GG. We say that graph GG is connected if for all u,v∈Vu,v\in V we have that uu and vv are connected. We say that G⁡[V′]G[V^{\prime}] for some V′⊆VV^{\prime}\subseteq V is a connected component of GG if G⁡[V′]G[V^{\prime}] is connected and for all v∈V∖V′v\in V\setminus V^{\prime} we have that G⁡[V′∪{v}]G[V^{\prime}\cup\{v\}] is not connected. We say that a path PP of length ℓ\ell in GG from vertex uu to vv is a shortest path if there is no path from uu to vv in GG of length ℓ−1\ell-1. The distance between uu and vv in GG is the length of a shortest path from uu to vv in GG and denoted dist⁡(u,v)\dist(u,v). If uu and vv are in different connected components of GG, then we set dist⁡(u,v)=∞\dist(u,v)=\infty. The diameter of a graph GG is the maximum distance between any two vertices that are in the same connected component, that is, diam⁡(G)=maxu,v∈V⁡(G)|dist⁡(u,v)≠∞⁡dist⁡(u,v)\diam(G)=\max_{u,v\in V(G)\mid\dist(u,v)\neq\infty}\dist(u,v).

A graph GG is planar if it can be embedded in the plane (drawn with points for vertices and curves for edges) without crossing edges. A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a unit disk graph if it has an intersection model consisting of disks of unit size, that is, there is a f:V→ℝf:V\rightarrow\mathbb{R} such that for all {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E it holds that |f⁡(u)−f⁡(v)|≤1|f(u)-f(v)|\leq 1. The set D={f⁡(v)∣v∈V}D=\{f(v)\mid v\in V\} is called the point set of GG. A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a grid if there exists a function f:V→[t]×[t′]f:V\rightarrow[t]\times[t^{\prime}] for some t,t′∈ℕt,t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N} such that for all {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E it holds that if f⁡(u)=(i,j)f(u)=(i,j) and f⁡(v)=(i′,j′)f(v)=(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}) then |i−i′|=1|i-i^{\prime}|=1 and j=j′j=j^{\prime}, or |j−j′|=1|j-j^{\prime}|=1 and i=i′i=i^{\prime}. Note that grids are planar graphs and unit disk graphs.

Problem Definition.

Assume we are given a graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) and two sets R,O⊆VR,O\subseteq V with R∩O=∅R\cap O=\emptyset. Here, RR denotes the starting positions of the main robots and OO denotes the starting positions of the obnoxious robots. We denote k=|R|k=|R| and ℓ=|O|\ell=|O|. Let m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O. We call a vector Mr=(v1,v2,v3,…,vm)M_{r}=(v_{1},v_{2},v_{3},\ldots,v_{m}) a movement for rr with mm steps if v1=rv_{1}=r and for all i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1] it holds that vi=vi+1v_{i}=v_{i+1} or {vi,vi+1}∈E\{v_{i},v_{i+1}\}\in E. Intuitively, in every step of a movement, the robot may stay on its current position or move to an adjacent vertex. The length len⁡(Mr)\len(M_{r}) of a movement Mr=(vi)i∈[m]M_{r}=(v_{i})_{i\in[m]} is len⁡(Mr)=|{i∈[m−1]∣vi≠vi+1}|\len(M_{r})=|\{i\in[m-1]\mid v_{i}\neq v_{i+1}\}|, that is, the number of steps in which rr moves to an adjacent vertex. We say that a movement MrM_{r} is trivial if len⁡(Mr)=0\len(M_{r})=0. We say that two movements Mr=(vi)i∈[m]M_{r}=(v_{i})_{i\in[m]} and Mr′=(vi′)i∈[m]M_{r^{\prime}}=(v^{\prime}_{i})_{i\in[m]} for some r,r′∈R∪Or,r^{\prime}\in R\cup O with mm steps each are collision-free if for all i∈[m]i\in[m] it holds that vi≠vi′v_{i}\neq v^{\prime}_{i} and for all i∈[m−1]i\in[m-1] it holds that {vi,vi+1}≠{vi′,vi+1′}\{v_{i},v_{i+1}\}\neq\{v^{\prime}_{i},v^{\prime}_{i+1}\}. Intuitively, robots collide if they occupy the same vertex in the same step or if they use the same edge (in opposite directions) to move to an adjacent vertex in the same step. A movement plan for R∪OR\cup O is a set ℳ={Mr∣r∈R∪O}\mathcal{M}=\{M_{r}\mid r\in R\cup O\} containing a movement for each robot in R∪OR\cup O with the same number of steps. The length of a movement plan len⁡(ℳ)\len(\mathcal{M}) is the sum of length of all movements in ℳ\mathcal{M}, that is, len⁡(ℳ)=∑Mr∈ℳlen⁡(Mr)\len(\mathcal{M})=\sum_{M_{r}\in\mathcal{M}}\len(M_{r}). We say that a movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} is collision-free if for all Mr,Mr′∈ℳM_{r},M_{r^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{M} with r≠r′r\neq r^{\prime} we have that the movements MrM_{r} and Mr′M_{r^{\prime}} are collision-free. The end-configuration of RR after a movement plan ℳ={Mr∣r∈R∪O}\mathcal{M}=\{M_{r}\mid r\in R\cup O\} is R⋆​(ℳ)={vm∣∃Mr∈ℳ​ s.t. ​r∈R​ and ​Mr=(vi)i∈[m]}R^{\star}(\mathcal{M})=\{v_{m}\mid\exists M_{r}\in\mathcal{M}\text{ s.t.\ }r\in R\text{ and }M_{r}=(v_{i})_{i\in[m]}\}, that is, the set of vertices that are occupied by robots in RR after all movements.

Let Π\Pi be a recursively enumerable graph property. We define the problem Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi as follows.

Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi Input: A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E), two sets R,O⊆VR,O\subseteq V with R∩O=∅R\cap O=\emptyset, and an integer c∈ℕc\in\mathbb{N}. Question: Is there a collision-free movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} for R∪OR\cup O such that len⁡(ℳ)≤c\len(\mathcal{M})\leq c and G​[R⋆​(ℳ)]∈ΠG[R^{\star}(\mathcal{M})]\in\Pi?

In this work, we will focus on the case of Π\Pi being the property of a graph to be connected. We call this problem Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity.

First Observations and Results.

Since Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi contains the problem of deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi as a special case, we immediately get the following.

Observation 10.

If deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi is NP-hard, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is NP-hard even if ℓ=0\ell=0 and c=0c=0.

If we do not require the movement plan to be collision-free, then we call the problem Movement to Π\Pi. A generalization of Movement to Π\Pi has been studied by Demaine et al. [11, 12]. We can observe that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi and Movement to Π\Pi coincide if ℓ=0\ell=0.

Lemma 11.

Let I=(G=(V,E),R,O,c)I=(G=(V,E),R,O,c) be an instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. If O=∅O=\emptyset, then II is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi if and only if II is a yes-instance of Movement to Π\Pi.

Proof.

If II is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi, then clearly it is also a yes-instance of Movement to Π\Pi. For the other direction, assume that II is a yes-instance of Movement to Π\Pi and let ℳ\mathcal{M} be a movement plan that is a solution for II. Assume that ℳ\mathcal{M} is not collision-free. Now let M=(v1,v2,…,vm)M=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{m}) and M′=(v1′,v2′,…,vm′′)M^{\prime}=(v^{\prime}_{1},v^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{m^{\prime}}) be two movements for robots r,r′∈Rr,r^{\prime}\in R, respectively, in ℳ\mathcal{M} that collide. Let tt be the step in which a collision happens, that is, vt=vt′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t}, or vt=vt−1′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t-1} and vt′=vt−1v^{\prime}_{t}=v_{t-1}. Consider the latter case first, that is, vt=vt−1′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t-1} and vt′=vt−1v^{\prime}_{t}=v_{t-1}. Here, instead of the robots swapping their position, they can “swap their identities” instead. Formally, we can define a new movement M⋆M^{\star} for robot rr which equals MM for the first t−1t-1 steps, and equals M′M^{\prime} for all subsequent steps, that is, M⋆=(v1,v2,…,vt−1,vt′,vt+1′,…,vm′′)M^{\star}=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{t-1},v^{\prime}_{t},v^{\prime}_{t+1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{m^{\prime}}). Analogously, we define a new movement for r′r^{\prime}. Clearly, the end-configuration of ℳ\mathcal{M} stays the same. By iterating this modification, we can eliminate all collisions of this type. Now consider the former case, that is, vt=vt′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t}. First consider the case that both rr and r′r^{\prime} moved to vt=vt′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t} in step tt, that is vt−1≠vtv_{t-1}\neq v_{t} and vt−1′≠vt′v^{\prime}_{t-1}\neq v^{\prime}_{t}. Then we create a new movement for rr where the movement from vt−1v_{t-1} to vtv_{t} happens one time step later. By iterating this modification, we can create a movement plan where no two robots simultaneously move to the same vertex. Now assume w.l.o.g. that robot rr moves to vtv_{t} in step tt, that is, vt−1≠vtv_{t-1}\neq v_{t} and robot r′r^{\prime} was already at vt=vt′v_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t} at the previous step, that is, vt′=vt−1′v^{\prime}_{t}=v^{\prime}_{t-1}. Furthermore, assume that tt is the latest step where such a collision happens. Then at some later time step t′>tt^{\prime}>t we must have that one of the robots moves away. Assume w.l.o.g. that r′r^{\prime} moves away first (if only rr moves away, they can “swap identities” according to the modification above). This implies that vt−1′=vt′=…=vt′−1v^{\prime}_{t-1}=v^{\prime}_{t}=\ldots=v_{t^{\prime}-1} in M′M^{\prime}. Then we can create a new movement M⋆M^{\star} for r′r^{\prime} that is equal to M′M^{\prime} until step t−1t-1 and then “skips” steps tt to t′−1t^{\prime}-1 and immediately moves to vt′′v^{\prime}_{t^{\prime}} at step tt and then continues with the steps of M′M^{\prime} from t′t^{\prime} onward, that is, M⋆=(v1′,v2′,…,vt−1′,vt′′,vt′+1′,…,vm′′)M^{\star}=(v^{\prime}_{1},v^{\prime}_{2},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{t-1},v^{\prime}_{t^{\prime}},v^{\prime}_{t^{\prime}+1},\ldots,v^{\prime}_{m^{\prime}}). Note that this may introduce new collisions, but it (strictly) shortens one of the movement vectors. It follows that iterating this modification will eventually eliminate all collisions. ∎

Lemma 11 implies that algorithmic results for Movement to Π\Pi carry over to Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi (and vice versa) if ℓ=0\ell=0. In particular, we get the following.

Theorem 12 ([12]).

If ℓ=0\ell=0, then Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by kk.

Due to the similarity of Movement to Π\Pi and Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi, the reductions behind some known hardness results for Movement to Π\Pi can be straightforwardly modified to work for Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. In particular, Demaine et al. [12] show that if Π\Pi is hereditary and does not contain all complete graphs and all empty graphs, then Movement to Π\Pi is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c even if ℓ=0\ell=0 via a reduction from the well-known Π\Pi-subgraph detection problem [33]. The reduction formalizes the intuition that already finding a suitable target location for the main robots is hard, rather than finding out in which way the robots move to that location. The reduction can be straightforwardly modified to yield the following result.

Theorem 13 ([12, 33]).

If Π\Pi is hereditary and does not contain all complete graphs and all empty graphs, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c even if ℓ=0\ell=0.

Demaine et al. [11] show that Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard even if ℓ=0\ell=0 via a reduction from Hamiltonian Path [32]. This reduction can be straightforwardly modified as well. If additionally we reduce from Hamiltonian Path on planar graphs [27], we obtain the following result.

Theorem 14 ([11]).

Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard even if ℓ=0\ell=0 and the input graph is planar.

If the main robots have prescribed destinations, that is, for each r∈Rr\in R there is a dr∈Vd_{r}\in V given as part of the input, and we ask for a collision free movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} (of length at most cc) that moves each robot in RR to its destination, that is, for each r∈Rr\in R we have Mr∈ℳM_{r}\in\mathcal{M} with Mr=(vi)i∈[m]M_{r}=(v_{i})_{i\in[m]} and vm=drv_{m}=d_{r}, then the problem is called Collision-Free Movement. A generalization of Collision-Free Movement has been studied by Deligkas et al. [10].

Observe that, given an instance (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi, if we can “guess” a destination vertex drd_{r} for each main robot r∈Rr\in R such that the subgraph of GG induced on the destination vertices has property Π\Pi, then we can reduce the problem of finding a collision-free movement plan of length at most cc to an instance of Collision-Free Movement. In particular, this gives us the following.

Observation 15.

If deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi is in NP, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is in NP.

Last but not least, we can observe that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi can be solved by a simple guess-and-check algorithm if deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi is polynomial-time solvable. We can iterate over all nO⁡(c)n^{O(c)} possibilities to pick cc moves and assign each one to one of the robots. Then we check whether this yields a collision-free movement plan and whether the end-configuration yields a subgraph with property Π\Pi. Hence, we get the following.

Theorem 16.

If deciding whether a graph has property Π\Pi is polynomial-time solvable, then Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is in XP when parameterized by cc.

4 Hardness Results

In this section, we give our main hardness results for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. We begin by proving Theorem 1 (restated below), that is, showing that the problem is W[1]-hard when parameterized by k+ck+c on general graphs. Afterwards, we investigate the cases where the input graph is a grids.

See 1

To prove Theorem 1, we present a parameterized reduction from Multicolored Clique [19]. Here, given an ℓ\ell-partite graph H=(W1⊎W2⊎…⊎Wℓ,F)H=(W_{1}\uplus W_{2}\uplus\ldots\uplus W_{\ell},F), we are asked whether HH contains a clique of size ℓ\ell. If v∈Wiv\in W_{i}, then we say that vv has color ii. Let Fi,jF_{i,j} denote the set of all edges between vertices from WiW_{i} and WjW_{j}. This problem is known to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by ℓ\ell [19].

Construction 1.

Given an instance H=(W1⊎W2⊎…⊎Wℓ,F)H=(W_{1}\uplus W_{2}\uplus\ldots\uplus W_{\ell},F) of Multicolored Clique, we construct an instance (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity as follows.

For each color combination i,ji,j with i<ji<j we create an edge selection gadget Gi,jG_{i,j}.

  • •

    For every edge e∈Fi,je\in F_{i,j} we add a vertex vev_{e}, place an obnoxious robot on it.

  • •

    We add three additional vertices v1,v2,v3v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}. We connect v1v_{1} to each vev_{e} with e∈Fi,je\in F_{i,j} and place a main robot on v1v_{1}. We connect v2v_{2} to each vev_{e} with e∈Fi,je\in F_{i,j} and place a main robot on v2v_{2}. We connect v3v_{3} to each vev_{e}.

For an illustration see Figure 7. For each color ii we create a validation gadget GiG_{i} as follows.

  • •

    For every vertex w∈Wiw\in W_{i} we create ℓ−1\ell-1 vertices w1,w2,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wℓw_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{i-1},w_{i+1},\ldots,w_{\ell} and connect them to a path (from w1w_{1} to wℓw_{\ell}).

  • •

    We add two vertices u1(i),u2(i)u^{(i)}_{1},u^{(i)}_{2} and place main robots on them. We connect u1(i)u^{(i)}_{1} to each w1w_{1} with w∈Wiw\in W_{i}. We connect u2(i)u^{(i)}_{2} to each wℓw_{\ell} with w∈Wiw\in W_{i}. We create a path on cc vertices, place main robots on each vertex, and connect one of the endpoints to u1(i)u^{(i)}_{1}, where we specify cc later. We create a second path on cc vertices, place main robots on each vertex, and connect one of the endpoints to u2(i)u^{(i)}_{2}.

The graph GG is now the disjoint union of the edge selection gadgets of all color combinations i,ji,j with i<ji<j and the verification gadgets of all colors ii. We connect the gadgets as follows. Let j=i+1≤ℓj=i+1\leq\ell, then we connect vertex u2(i)u^{(i)}_{2} from the verification gadget GiG_{i} and vertex u1(j)u^{(j)}_{1} from the verification gadget GjG_{j} with an edge. Finally, let e={w,w′}∈Fi,je=\{w,w^{\prime}\}\in F_{i,j} such that w∈Wiw\in W_{i} and w′∈Wjw^{\prime}\in W_{j}. We connect vertex vev_{e} from the edge selection gadget Gi,jG_{i,j} with vertex wjw_{j} from the verification gadget GiG_{i}. Then we subdivide ℓ2\ell^{2} times the edge {ve,wj}\{v_{e},w_{j}\}. We connect vertex vev_{e} from the edge selection gadget Gi,jG_{i,j} with vertex wi′w^{\prime}_{i} from the verification gadget GjG_{j}. Then we subdivide ℓ2\ell^{2} times the edge {ve,wi′}\{v_{e},w^{\prime}_{i}\}. Finally, we set c=(2​ℓ2+3)​(ℓ2)c=(2\ell^{2}+3)\binom{\ell}{2}.

This finished the construction, which can clearly be performed in polynomial time. Note that the number of main robots is in O⁡(ℓ4)O(\ell^{4}) and c∈O⁡(ℓ4)c\in O(\ell^{4}). Now we prove the correctness of the reduction, that is, the constructed instance (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity if and only if HH is a yes-instance of Multicolored Clique. This together with the above observations yields Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1.

Let be H=(W1⊎W2⊎…⊎Wℓ,F)H=(W_{1}\uplus W_{2}\uplus\ldots\uplus W_{\ell},F) an instance of Multicolored Clique and let (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) be an instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity created from HH by Construction 1.

(⇒):(\Rightarrow): Assume that HH is a yes-instance of Multicolored Clique and we are given a clique X⊆V⁡(H)X\subseteq V(H). We construct a collision-free movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} of length cc for (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) as follows.

For each color combination i,ji,j with i<ji<j let e={w,w′}∈Fi,je=\{w,w^{\prime}\}\in F_{i,j} such that w∈Wiw\in W_{i}, w′∈Wjw^{\prime}\in W_{j}, and w,w′∈Xw,w^{\prime}\in X. We move the obnoxious robot on vertex vev_{e} of the edge selection gadget Gi,jG_{i,j} to vertex v3v_{3} of the edge selection gadget Gi,jG_{i,j}. By Construction 1, we have that vev_{e} is connected to vertex wjw_{j} from the verification gadget GiG_{i} via a path of length ℓ2+1\ell^{2}+1 and is connected to vertex wi′w^{\prime}_{i} from the verification gadget GjG_{j} via a path of length ℓ2+1\ell^{2}+1. We move the main robot on v1v_{1} to wjw_{j} via vev_{e} and the connecting path, and we move the main robot on v2v_{2} to wi′w^{\prime}_{i} via vev_{e} and the connecting path. Note that this is collision-free and takes 2​ℓ2+22\ell^{2}+2 moves. This finishes the description of the movement plan. Note that it uses 2​ℓ2+32\ell^{2}+3 moves for every edge selection gadget and hence c=(2​ℓ2+3)​(ℓ2)c=(2\ell^{2}+3)\binom{\ell}{2} moves in total.

It remains to show that the end-configuration forms a connected subgraph. To this end, note that for some fixed ii, all edges of a color combination that contains ii that are contained in the clique XX have the same endpoint in WiW_{i}. Let that endpoint be w∈Wiw\in W_{i} Hence, we have that in the verification gadget for color ii, one main robot is moved to each of w1,w2,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wℓw_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{i-1},w_{i+1},\ldots,w_{\ell} and hence vertices u1(i),u2(i)u^{(i)}_{1},u^{(i)}_{2} (which have main robots on them) are connected via a path that has a main robot on each vertex. Since this is the case for every verification gadget and there are no main robots left in the edge selection gadgets, we have that the main robots form a connected subgraph.

(⇐):(\Leftarrow): Assume that (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity and we are given a collision-free movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} of length cc that is a solution for (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c). We construct a clique of size ℓ\ell in HH as follows.

Assume that ℳ\mathcal{M} is a movement plan with a minimum number of moves. First, observe the following. For each verification gadget for a color ii it holds that the main robots on u1(i),u2(i)u^{(i)}_{1},u^{(i)}_{2} do not move. Recall that by Construction 1, each of the vertices is connected to a path of length cc that has main robots on every vertex. Moving the main robot on u1(i)u^{(i)}_{1} or u2(i)u^{(i)}_{2} breaks the connection to the main robots on the respective path. To reestablish connection, either the robot needs to move back to u1(i)u^{(i)}_{1} or u2(i)u^{(i)}_{2}, respectively, which does not happen in a movement plan with a minimum number of moves, or all robots on the path need to be moved by at least one step, which costs more than cc moves in total and hence cannot happen in a solution. It follows that only the 2​(ℓ2)2\binom{\ell}{2} main robots in edge selection gadgets move. Furthermore, notice that the paths between verification gadgets and edge selection gadgets have length ℓ2>2​(ℓ2)\ell^{2}>2\binom{\ell}{2}. It follows that a connection cannot be established via those paths since there are not enough main robots that can move. We can conclude that for each color ii the vertices w1,w2,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wℓw_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{i-1},w_{i+1},\ldots,w_{\ell} for some w∈Wiw\in W_{i} need to be occupied by main robots in the end-configuration. The distance of a starting position of a main robot in an edge selection gadget to such a vertex is at least ℓ2+2\ell^{2}+2. Furthermore, all neighboring vertices of starting position of a main robot in an edge selection gadget are occupied by obnoxious robots that need to be moved away first. Note that for each edge selection gadget, there are at most one move available to do this. It follows that in each edge selection gadget, we move exactly one obnoxious robot from some vev_{e} to the v3v_{3} vertex of that gadget. We say that edge ee is “selected”. Furthermore, we have that for each color ii, exactly the vertices w1,w2,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wℓw_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{i-1},w_{i+1},\ldots,w_{\ell} for some w∈Wiw\in W_{i} are occupied by main robots in the end-configuration, which each were moved there with exactly ℓ2+2\ell^{2}+2 moves.

Let XX be the set of all endpoints of selected edges. We claim that XX forms a clique of size ℓ\ell in HH. Note that XX contains at least one vertex of each color, hence |X|≥ℓ|X|\geq\ell. In the remainder, we show that also |X|≤ℓ|X|\leq\ell. Note that this implies that XX is a clique, since for each color ii we have that all edges of a color combination that contains ii have the same endpoint of color ii. Assume for contradiction that w,w′∈Xw,w^{\prime}\in X with w,w′∈Wiw,w^{\prime}\in W_{i} for some color ii. Then there are selected edges e,e′e,e^{\prime} such that ww is an endpoint of ee and w′w^{\prime} is an endpoint of e′e^{\prime}. Consider the edge selection gadgets where ee and e′e^{\prime} were selected. Both correspond to a color combination that involves ii, so both are connected to the verification gadget of color ii. If two main robots from one of the gadgets are moved into the verification gadget of color ii, this involves at least ℓ2+3\ell^{2}+3 moves. Hence, by arguments made above, this is not possible in a solution. We can conclude that from both edge selection gadgets, one main robot must be moved to the verification gadget of color ii with ℓ2+2\ell^{2}+2 moves. Then, however, the main robots are moved to vertices wjw_{j} and wj′′w^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}} for some j,j′j,j^{\prime} in the verification gadget for color ii. This is a contradiction to the observation above, that for color ii the vertices w1,w2,…,wi−1,wi+1,…,wℓw_{1},w_{2},\ldots,w_{i-1},w_{i+1},\ldots,w_{\ell} for some w∈Wiw\in W_{i} need to be occupied by main robots in the end-configuration. We can conclude that XX is a clique in HH. ∎

Hardness on Grids.

Now we prove Theorem 2 (restated below), that is, we show that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard if the input graph is a grid, even if there are only two main robots. To this end, we first give a reduction that produces a planar graph, and then we show how to modify the construction such that we obtain a grid.

See 2

To prove Theorem 2, we present a polynomial-time reduction from Linked Planar 3-SAT [37]. Here, we are given a Boolean formula ϕ\phi in 3-CNF with clause set YY and variable set XX, and a graph H=(Y∪X,F)H=(Y\cup X,F) such that the following holds:

  • •

    Graph HH is the union of a Hamiltonian cycle that first visits all elements of XX and then all elements of YY, and the incidence graph of ϕ\phi (i.e., the graph on Y∪XY\cup X where c∈Yc\in Y and x∈Xx\in X are connected by an edge if and only if variable xx appears on clause cc).

  • •

    Graph HH is planar and w.l.o.g. there is an embedding where each edge between a clause and a variable that appears negated in the clause is inside the cycle, and each edge between a clause and a variable that appears non-negated in the clause is outside of the cycle.

  • •

    Each variable appears in at most three clauses.

This problem is known to be NP-hard even if HH together with its embedding are given in the input [37]. Note that the Hamiltonian cycle can easily be computed from HH.

In the following, we first describe a construction that, given an instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT, produces an instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity with a planar graph. Later, we describe how to modify the instance such that the graph is a grid.

Construction 2.

Given an instance (ϕ,H)(\phi,H) of Linked Planar 3-SAT, we construct an instance (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity with k=2k=2 as follows. Let the variables XX and clauses YY in ϕ\phi be ordered in the way they appear in the Hamiltonian cycle in HH.

For each variable x∈Xx\in X, we create a variable gadget Gx=(Vx,Ex)G_{x}=(V_{x},E_{x}) with

  • •

    Vx={v1x,v2x,v3x,v4x,u1x,u2x,u3x,w1x,w2x,w3x}V_{x}=\{v_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x},v_{4}^{x},u_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x},w_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x}\}, and

  • •

    Ex={{v1x,v2x},{v2x,v3x},{v3x,u1x},{u1x,u2x},{u2x,u3x},{u3x,v4x},{v3x,w3x},{w3x,w2x},E_{x}=\{\{v_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x}\},\{v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x}\},\{v_{3}^{x},u_{1}^{x}\},\{u_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x}\},\{u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x}\},\{u_{3}^{x},v_{4}^{x}\},\{v_{3}^{x},w_{3}^{x}\},\{w_{3}^{x},w_{2}^{x}\},

    {w2x,w1x},{w1x,v4x}}\{w_{2}^{x},w_{1}^{x}\},\{w_{1}^{x},v_{4}^{x}\}\}.

Furthermore, we place obnoxious robots on the vertices v1x,v2x,v3xv_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x}. For an illustration of the variable gadget see Figure 8.

We construct the graph GG of the Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity instance by first taking the graph HH and replacing each vertex corresponding to a variable, say xx, with variable gadget GxG_{x} in the following way. If two vertices corresponding to variables x,yx,y are adjacent in HH, that is, they appear consecutive in the ordering (first xx and then yy), then we add edge {v4x,v1y}\{v_{4}^{x},v_{1}^{y}\} to GG. Let xx be the last variable in the ordering and let cc be the first clause in the ordering, then we add edge {v4x,vc}\{v_{4}^{x},v^{c}\} to GG and subdivide it s+2s+2 times, where s=|X|+|Y|s=|X|+|Y|. For each clause c∈Cc\in C we add call the vertex corresponding to it vcv^{c} and place an obnoxious robot on vcv^{c}. Let variable xx appear in clauses c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}. Then the vertex xx in HH is connected to vertices vc1,vc2,vc3v^{c_{1}},v^{c_{2}},v^{c_{3}} in HH. Let w.l.o.g. the order c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} be the linearization of the cyclic ordering in which the edges incident with xx to the vertices c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} are embedded around xx in the planar embedding of HH, such that all clauses in which xx appears non-negated are ordered before the clauses in which xx appears negated. For i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}, if xx appears in cic_{i} non-negated, then we connect uixu_{i}^{x} with vciv^{c_{i}} with an edge and subdivide the edge ss times. Furthermore, we place an obnoxious robot on each vertex created by a subdivision. If xx appears in cic_{i} negated, then we connect wixw_{i}^{x} with vciv^{c_{i}} with an edge and subdivide the edge ss times. Furthermore, we place an obnoxious robot on each vertex created by a subdivision. Finally, we add two vertices r1,r2r_{1},r_{2} to GG and place a main robot on each of them. Let xx be the first variable in the ordering, then we add edge {r1,v1x}\{r_{1},v_{1}^{x}\} to GG. Let cc be the last clause in the ordering, then we add edge {r2,vc}\{r_{2},v^{c}\} to GG. For an illustration, see Figure 9. Finally, we set c=16⋅|X|+(s+2)⋅(|Y|+1)+1c=16\cdot|X|+(s+2)\cdot(|Y|+1)+1. We will assume in the proofs of correctness that s2/4>cs^{2}/4>c. Note that this is clearly the case if |X||X| and |Y||Y| are sufficiently large.

This finishes the construction, which can clearly be performed in polynomial time. It is fairly straightforward to check that the constructed graph GG is planar.

Observation 17.

The graph GG obtained from Construction 2 is planar.

Proof.

For an illustration, see Figure 9. Recall that HH is the union of a Hamiltonian cycle that first visits all variables XX and then all clauses YY, and the incidence graph of ϕ\phi. Consider a planar embedding of HH where each edge between a clause and a variable that appears negated in the clause is inside the cycle, and each edge between a clause and a variable that appears non-negated in the clause is outside of the cycle. In Construction 2, when we replace the vertex corresponding to a variable xx with variable gadget GxG_{x}, we can arrange it such that vertices u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} point towards the outside of the cycle and w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x} to the inside. The gadget GxG_{x} itself is clearly planar. Now we can embed the paths in GG connecting the clause vertices with the variable gadgets along the edges between clauses and variables in HH. Note that in the construction of GG, when we connect the variable gadgets with the clause vertices, we connect clause vertices to vertices of the variable gadget in the same cyclic ordering as the edges around the corresponding variable in HH. It follows that we can embed the paths connecting variable gadgets and clause vertices in GG in a planar way. Finally, vertices r1,r2r_{1},r_{2} and their incident edges can clearly be embedded in a planar way. ∎

Next, we show correctness of the reduction, that is, the constructed instance (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity if and only if (ϕ,H)(\phi,H) is a yes-instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT.

Lemma 18.

If (ϕ,H)(\phi,H) is a yes-instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT, then (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity.

Proof.

Assume we are given a satisfying assignment for ϕ\phi. We create the following movement plan.

  • •

    We iterate over the variables in some arbitrary but fixed order. Let xx be a variable. If xx is set to true, then we move the three obnoxious robots on v1x,v2x,v3xv_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x} to w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x} in a collision-free way using 9 moves: We first move the robot on v3xv_{3}^{x} to w3xw_{3}^{x}, then we move the robot on v2xv_{2}^{x} to w2xw_{2}^{x}, and finally we move the robot on v1xv_{1}^{x} to w1xw_{1}^{x}. It is straightforward to check that this requires 9 moves and is collision-free. If xx is set to false, then we move the three obnoxious robots on v1x,v2x,v3xv_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x} to u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} in an analogous way. Doing this for each variable requires 9⋅|X|9\cdot|X| moves in total.

  • •

    Let zz be the last variable in the ordering (implied by the Hamiltonian cycle). We now move r1r_{1} to v4zv_{4}^{z}. Note that in each variable gadget for some variable xx, the vertices v1x,v2x,v3x,v4xv_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x},v_{4}^{x} are not occupied by any robot. Furthermore, either vertices u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} or vertices w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x} are not occupied by any robot. It follows that we can move r1r_{1} collision-free to v4zv_{4}^{z} using 7⋅|X|+17\cdot|X|+1 moves.

  • •

    Now for each clause cc we identify a literal ℓ\ell that satisfies the clause. Let xx be the variable of literal ℓ\ell. If xx appears in ℓ\ell non-negated, then by construction we have that vcv^{c} is connected by a path of length (s+1)(s+1) to one of the vertices u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} and no other literal of any other clause is connected to the same vertex as ℓ\ell. Furthermore, we have that these vertices are not occupied by any robot. Let vcv^{c} be connected to uixu_{i}^{x} with i∈[3]i\in[3]. The vertex vcv^{c} as well as all inner vertices on the path of length (s+1)(s+1) from vcv^{c} to uixu_{i}^{x} are occupied by obnoxious robots. We move all robots towards uixu_{i}^{x} by one step, starting with the one closest to uixu_{i}^{x} and ending with the one occupying vcv^{c}. This takes (s+1)(s+1) moves and is clearly collision-free. Afterwards, vertex vcv^{c} is not occupied by any vertex. If xx appears in ℓ\ell negated, we have an analogous situation with vertices w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x} instead of u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x}. Doing this for each clause requires (s+1)⋅|Y|(s+1)\cdot|Y| moves in total.

  • •

    Let c⋆c^{\star} be the last clause in the ordering (implied by the Hamiltonian cycle). We now move r1r_{1} from v4zv_{4}^{z} to vc⋆v^{c^{\star}}. This is collision-free since, after the previous moves, all vertices corresponding to clauses are not occupied by any robot, and it requires |Y|+s+2|Y|+s+2 moves.

After the above-described movement plan, main robot r1r_{1} occupies vertex vc⋆v^{c^{\star}} and main robot r2r_{2} still occupies its starting location. Since these two vertices are connected, we have that the end-configuration of the movement plan forms a connected subgraph. Furthermore, the movement plan clearly has length 16⋅|X|+(s+2)⋅(|Y|+1)+116\cdot|X|+(s+2)\cdot(|Y|+1)+1. ∎

Lemma 19.

If (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity, then (ϕ,H)(\phi,H) is a yes-instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT.

Proof.

Assume we are given a movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} that is a solution to (G,R,O,c)(G,R,O,c). We create a satisfying assignment for ϕ\phi as follows.

First, we start with the following observation: If a main robot moves (collision-free) along one of the paths of length (s+1)(s+1) from a vertex of a variable gadget to a clause vertex, all obnoxious robots need to move out of the way. This requires at least 2⋅∑i=1⌊s+1⌋i>s2/4>c2\cdot\sum_{i=1}^{\lfloor s+1\rfloor}i>s^{2}/4>c moves. Hence, we can conclude that in the movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M}, no main robot moves along such a path. It follows that each variable gadget is traversed by one of the main robots, and each clause vertex is traversed by one of the main robots. In particular, we can conclude that the main robots make at least 7⋅|X|+|Y|+s+37\cdot|X|+|Y|+s+3 moves.

We can conclude the following: In each variable gadget, the three obnoxious robots need to be moved such that one of the main robots can pass through the gadget. Moving them inside the gadget to u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} or w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x} requires 9 moves. Moving them in any other way that allows a main robot to pass (e.g. to an adjacent gadget) costs strictly more than 9 moves. Hence, at least 9⋅|X|9\cdot|X| moves are required to move obnoxious robots in the variable gadgets.

Now consider the clause vertices. Moving the obnoxious robot away from the clause vertex requires either moving each vertex on one of the paths of length (s+1)(s+1) be one step and hence requires (s+1)(s+1) moves in total, or moving the obnoxious robot into a path connected to a different clause vertex, , which requires at least (s+2)(s+2) moves, or moving the obnoxious robot into a variable gadget, which also requires at least (s+2)(s+2) moves. Hence, at least (s+1)⋅|Y|(s+1)\cdot|Y| moves are required to move obnoxious robots away from the clause vertices.

Adding up the above-derived lower bounds for the required moves yields exactly cc. We can conclude that in each variable gadget, the three obnoxious robots move to either u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x} or w1x,w2x,w3xw_{1}^{x},w_{2}^{x},w_{3}^{x}. Furthermore, for each clause vertex, all robots from the vertex along one of the paths of length (s+1)(s+1) to a variable gadget are moved by one step each.

We construct an assignment for the variables in XX as follows. For each x∈Xx\in X, if three obnoxious robots move to u1x,u2x,u3xu_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x}, then we set xx to true. Otherwise, we set xx to false. We claim that this is a satisfying assignment for ϕ\phi.

Assume for contradiction that this is not a satisfying assignment. Then there is a clause cc that is not satisfied. Consider the corresponding clause vertex vcv^{c}. If none of cc’s literals are satisfied, then by construction the vertices of the variable gadgets that are connected to vcv^{c} by paths of length (s+1)(s+1) are occupied by obnoxious robots. It follows that at least (s+2)(s+2) moves are necessary to move the obnoxious robot from vcv^{c}. Then, however, by the arguments given above, the total number of moves is strictly larger than cc, a contradiction. ∎

From 17, 18 and 19 follows that Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity is NP-hard even if k=2k=2 and the input graph is planar. In the following, we show how to modify Construction 2 to produce a graph that is a grid.

First, we argue that we can find an alternative embedding for GG by “unfolding” it, such that r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} lie on the outer face, see Figure 10 for an “unfolded” version of Figure 9. More formally, we can “break” the Hamiltonian cycle in HH between the first variable vertex and the last clause vertex, creating a Hamiltonian path that first visits all variable vertices and then all clause vertices. We can draw this path along a horizontal line. Then all edges that were outside the cycle are now above the path, and all edges inside the cycle are now below the path. We take this embedding as a starting point to construct a modified graph G′G^{\prime} that is a grid (together with an embedding that shows this). Note that there are three main obstacles to overcome:

  • •

    The clause vertices in GG may have degree 5, which is not possible in a grid. Hence, we have to modify the vertices to “clause gadgets” that are grids.

  • •

    All paths connecting clause gadgets to variable gadgets need to have the same length in order for the reduction to work.

  • •

    The path between the last variable gadget and the first clause gadget has to be sufficiently long (that is, longer than any path from a clause gadget to a variable gadget) for the reduction to work.

Formally, we construct G′G^{\prime} as follows.

Construction 3.

Given an instance (ϕ,H)(\phi,H) of Linked Planar 3-SAT, we construct an instance (G′=(V′,E′),R′,O′,c′)(G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}),R^{\prime},O^{\prime},c^{\prime}) of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity with k=2k=2 as follows. Let the variables XX and clauses YY in ϕ\phi be ordered in the way they appear in the Hamiltonian cycle in HH.

For each variable x∈Xx\in X, we create a variable gadget Gx′=(Vx′,Ex′)G^{\prime}_{x}=(V^{\prime}_{x},E^{\prime}_{x}) with

  • •

    Ex′={{v1x,v2x},{v2x,v3x},{v3x,v4x},{v4x,v5x},{v5x,u1x},{u1x,u2x},{u2x,u3x},{u3x,u4x},E^{\prime}_{x}=\{\{v_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x}\},\{v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x}\},\{v_{3}^{x},v_{4}^{x}\},\{v_{4}^{x},v_{5}^{x}\},\{v_{5}^{x},u_{1}^{x}\},\{u_{1}^{x},u_{2}^{x}\},\{u_{2}^{x},u_{3}^{x}\},\{u_{3}^{x},u_{4}^{x}\},

    {u4x,u5x},{u5x,v6x},{v5x,w5x},{w5x,w4x},{w4x,w3x},{w3x,w2x},{w2x,w1x},\{u_{4}^{x},u_{5}^{x}\},\{u_{5}^{x},v_{6}^{x}\},\{v_{5}^{x},w_{5}^{x}\},\{w_{5}^{x},w_{4}^{x}\},\{w_{4}^{x},w_{3}^{x}\},\{w_{3}^{x},w_{2}^{x}\},\{w_{2}^{x},w_{1}^{x}\},

    {w1x,v6x},{v6x,v7x}}\{w_{1}^{x},v_{6}^{x}\},\{v_{6}^{x},v_{7}^{x}\}\}.

Furthermore, we place obnoxious robots on the vertices v1x,v2x,v3x,v4x,v5xv_{1}^{x},v_{2}^{x},v_{3}^{x},v_{4}^{x},v_{5}^{x}. For an illustration of the variable gadget see Figure 11.

For each variable c∈Yc\in Y, we create a variable gadget Gc′=(Vc′,Ec′)G^{\prime}_{c}=(V^{\prime}_{c},E^{\prime}_{c}) with

  • •

    Vc′={v1c,v2c,v3c,v4c,v5c,v6c,u1c,u2c,u3c,u4c,u5c,w1c,w2c,w3c,w4c,w5c}V^{\prime}_{c}=\{v_{1}^{c},v_{2}^{c},v_{3}^{c},v_{4}^{c},v_{5}^{c},v_{6}^{c},u_{1}^{c},u_{2}^{c},u_{3}^{c},u_{4}^{c},u_{5}^{c},w_{1}^{c},w_{2}^{c},w_{3}^{c},w_{4}^{c},w_{5}^{c}\}, and

  • •

    Ec′={{v1c,v2c},{v2c,v3c},{v3c,v4c},{v4c,v5c},{v3c,u3c},{u1c,u2c},{u2c,u3c},{u3c,u4c},E^{\prime}_{c}=\{\{v_{1}^{c},v_{2}^{c}\},\{v_{2}^{c},v_{3}^{c}\},\{v_{3}^{c},v_{4}^{c}\},\{v_{4}^{c},v_{5}^{c}\},\{v_{3}^{c},u_{3}^{c}\},\{u_{1}^{c},u_{2}^{c}\},\{u_{2}^{c},u_{3}^{c}\},\{u_{3}^{c},u_{4}^{c}\},

    {u4c,u5c},{v3c,w3c},{w5c,w4c},{w4c,w3c},{w3c,w2c},{w2c,w1c}}\{u_{4}^{c},u_{5}^{c}\},\{v_{3}^{c},w_{3}^{c}\},\{w_{5}^{c},w_{4}^{c}\},\{w_{4}^{c},w_{3}^{c}\},\{w_{3}^{c},w_{2}^{c}\},\{w_{2}^{c},w_{1}^{c}\}\}.

Furthermore, we place obnoxious robots on the vertices v3c,u1c,u2c,u3c,u4c,u5c,w1c,w2c,w3c,w4c,w5cv_{3}^{c},u_{1}^{c},u_{2}^{c},u_{3}^{c},u_{4}^{c},u_{5}^{c},w_{1}^{c},w_{2}^{c},w_{3}^{c},w_{4}^{c},w_{5}^{c}. For an illustration of the clause gadget see Figure 12.

We construct the graph G′G^{\prime} of the Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity instance by first taking the graph HH and replacing each vertex corresponding to a variable, say xx, with variable gadget Gx′G^{\prime}_{x} in the following way. If two vertices corresponding to variables x,yx,y are adjacent in HH, that is, they appear consecutive in the ordering (first xx and then yy), then we add edge {v7x,v1y}\{v_{7}^{x},v_{1}^{y}\} to G′G^{\prime}. Let xx be the last variable in the ordering and let cc be the first clause in the ordering, then we add edge {v7x,v1c}\{v_{7}^{x},v_{1}^{c}\} to G′G^{\prime} and subdivide it s+4s+4 times, where s=90⋅(|X|+|Y|)−4s=90\cdot(|X|+|Y|)-4. For each clause c∈Cc\in C we replace the corresponding vertex with clause gadget Gc′G^{\prime}_{c} in the following way. If two clauses c,c′c,c^{\prime} appear consecutive in the ordering (first cc and then c′c^{\prime}), then we add edge {v6c,v1c′}\{v_{6}^{c},v_{1}^{c^{\prime}}\} to GG. Let variable xx appear in clauses c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3}. Then the vertex xx in HH is connected to vertices vc1,vc2,vc3v^{c_{1}},v^{c_{2}},v^{c_{3}} in HH. Let w.l.o.g. the order c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} be the linearization of the clockwise cyclic ordering in which the edges incident with xx to the vertices c1,c2,c3c_{1},c_{2},c_{3} are embedded around xx in the planar embedding of HH, such that all clauses in which xx appears non-negated are ordered before the clauses in which xx appears negated. This we can do by arranging the path snake-like, going 4 grid-cells up and 4 grid-cells down, as depicted in Figure 13.
