5 Collision Free Movement on Grids

In this section, we present parameterized algorithms for Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi parameterized by k+ck+c on grids. Specifically, we give kernelization algorithms that produce problems kernels of size O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) for Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi and O⁡(min⁡{k⋅c2,k2+c2})O(\min\{k\cdot c^{2},k^{2}+c^{2}\}) for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. This means, if c∈ω⁡(k)c\in\omega(\sqrt{k}), we have a strictly better kernel size for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. These kernelization algorithms can then e.g. be combined with Theorem 16 to obtain an algorithm with a running time in (k⋅c)O⁡(c)+nO⁡(1)(k\cdot c)^{O(c)}+n^{O(1)}.

Kernelization.

To obtain the kernelization results, we give a number of straightforward reduction rules. A reduction rule is a description of a procedure that takes a problem instance as input and outputs an instance of the same problem. We say that a reduction rule is safe, if it holds that the input instance is a yes-instance if and only if the output instance is a yes-instance. First, we prove Theorem 3 (restated below).

See 3

To prove Theorem 3, we present the following simple reduction rule. Essentially, it allows us to remove vertices that are too far away from all main robots. The intuition here is that if a vertex vv has distance more than cc to any main robot starting location, then it cannot be visited by any main robot, and it also cannot be visited by any obnoxious robot that needs to move in order to avoid collision.

Reduction Rule 1.

Let (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) be an instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. If there is a v∈Vv\in V such that for all r∈Rr\in R it holds that distG⁡(v,r)>c\dist_{G}(v,r)>c, then remove vv from GG (and from OO, if it is contained in OO).

Reduction Rule 1 can clearly be applied in polynomial time and it will also be useful in the algorithms we present in later sections. Next, we prove that it can be safely applied.

Lemma 21.

Reduction Rule 1 is safe.

Proof.

Assume for contradiction that there is a vertex vv that Reduction Rule 1 would remove and to or from which a robot is moved in a solution to the instance. Assume that the solution has a minimum number of movements. Note that this cannot be a main robot, since all of them have distance more than cc to vv and hence cannot be moved to vv. It follows that an obnoxious robot is moved to vv (or moved away from vv). In a solution with a minimum number of movements, an obnoxious robot is only moved to avoid a collision with a main robot or another obnoxious robot. In the latter case, this property holds recursively for the other obnoxious robot. We can conclude that in the end-configuration, there is a path from vv to a vertex v′v^{\prime} with a main robot such that all vertices of the path (except v′v^{\prime}) have obnoxious robots on them an each one has been moved by at least one step. Let ℓ′\ell^{\prime} be the number of obnoxious robots that have been moved. Then the distance of v′v^{\prime} to any main robot starting location is at least c−ℓ′+1c-\ell^{\prime}+1. It follows that moving a main robot to v′v^{\prime} and moving the ℓ′\ell^{\prime} obnoxious robots by one step each requires more that cc movements in total, a contradiction. ∎

Now we can prove Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

We apply Reduction Rule 1 exhaustively, which can clearly be done in polynomial time. By Lemma 21 we have that the rule is safe. The definition of Reduction Rule 1 implies that we keep a ball of radius cc around every vertex that has a main robot. In a grid, a ball of radius cc around a vertex contains O⁡(c2)O(c^{2}) vertices. It follows that after exhaustively applying Reduction Rule 1, the remaining graph GG has O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) vertices. ∎

Now we refine the kernelization algorithm for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity by introducing some additional reduction rules with which we can achieve a smaller kernel if k<c2k<c^{2}. This allows us to prove Theorem 4 (restated below).

See 4

To show Theorem 4, we introduce an additional reduction rule. Informally, this rule says that if a vertex vv is too far away (distance more than c+kc+k) from some main robot rr’s starting location, then is is irrelevant.

Reduction Rule 2.

Let (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) be an instance of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. If there is a v∈V∖Rv\in V\setminus R such that there exists r∈Rr\in R such that distG⁡(v,r)>c+k\dist_{G}(v,r)>c+k, then remove vv from GG (and from OO, if it is contained in OO).

Reduction Rule 2 can clearly be applied in polynomial time. Next we prove that it is safe.

Lemma 22.

Reduction Rule 2 is safe.

Proof.

Assume for contradiction that there is a vertex vv that Reduction Rule 2 would remove and to or from which a robot is moved in a solution to the instance. Assume that the solution has a minimum number of movements. Let r∈Rr\in R such that distG⁡(v,r)>c+k\dist_{G}(v,r)>c+k. Assume that an obnoxious robot is moved to vv (or moved away from vv). In a solution with a minimum number of movements, an obnoxious robot is only moved to avoid a collision with a main robot or another obnoxious robot. In the latter case, this property holds recursively for the other obnoxious robot. We can conclude that in the end-configuration, there is a path from vv to a vertex v′v^{\prime} with a main robot such that all vertices of the path (except v′v^{\prime}) have obnoxious robots on them an each one has been moved by at least one step. Let ℓ′\ell^{\prime} be the number of obnoxious robots that have been moved. If a main robot is moved to or from vv, set ℓ′=0\ell^{\prime}=0 and v=v′v=v^{\prime} in the following argument. Then the distance of v′v^{\prime} to rr is at least c+k−ℓ′+1c+k-\ell^{\prime}+1. Note that at most kk vertices on any path from v′v^{\prime} to rr can have main robots on them. It follows that connecting the main robot with starting location rr to the main robot on v′v^{\prime} and moving the ℓ′\ell^{\prime} obnoxious robots by one step each requires more that cc movements in total, a contradiction. ∎

Now we can prove Theorem 4.

Proof of Theorem 4.

We apply Reduction Rules 1 and 2 exhaustively, which can clearly be done in polynomial time. By Lemmas 21 and 22 we have that the rules are safe. By Theorem 3 we know that after exhaustively applying Reduction Rule 1, the remaining graph GG has O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) vertices. After applying Reduction Rule 2 we have that in particular, for any fixed r∈Rr\in R, we have that for all v∈V∖Rv\in V\setminus R it holds that distG⁡(v,r)≤c+k\dist_{G}(v,r)\leq c+k. It follows that we keep a ball of radius c+kc+k around rr that contains all vertices except possibly some vertices in RR. In a grid, a ball of radius c+kc+k around a vertex contains O⁡(c2+k2)O(c^{2}+k^{2}) vertices. It follows that after exhaustively applying Reduction Rule 2, the remaining graph GG has O⁡(k2+c2)O(k^{2}+c^{2}) vertices. The theorem statement follows. ∎

Kernelization Lower Bounds.

Now we present several kernelization lower bounds. We use the popular OR-cross-compositions framework [4, 25] to refute the existence of a polynomial kernel for a parameterized problem under the assumption that coNP ⊈\not\subseteq NP/poly, the negation of which would cause a collapse of the polynomial-time hierarchy to the third level. In order to formally define OR-cross-compositions, we introduce equivalence relations first. An equivalence relation RR on the instances of some problem LL is a polynomial equivalence relation if

  1. 1.

    one can decide for every two instances in time polynomial in their sizes whether they belong to the same equivalence class, and

  2. 2.

    for each finite set SS of instances, RR partitions the set into at most (maxx∈S⁡|x|)𝒪⁡(1)(\max_{x\in S}|x|)^{\mathcal{O}(1)} equivalence classes.

An OR-cross-composition of a problem L⊆{0,1}∗L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*} into a parameterized problem PP (with respect to a polynomial equivalence relation RR on the instances of LL) is an algorithm that takes tt RR-equivalent instances x1,…,xtx_{1},\ldots,x_{t} of LL and constructs in time polynomial in ∑i=1t|xi|\sum_{i=1}^{t}|x_{i}| an instance (y,k)(y,k) of PP such that

  1. 1.

    k≤(maxi∈[t]⁡|xi|+log⁡t)O⁡(1)k\leq(\max_{i\in[t]}|x_{i}|+\log t)^{O(1)}, and

  2. 2.

    (y,k)(y,k) is a yes-instance of PP if and only if there is an i∈[t]i\in[t] s.t. xix_{i} is a yes-instance of LL.

If an NP-hard problem LL OR-cross-composes into a parameterized problem PP, then PP does not admit a polynomial kernel, unless coNP ⊆\subseteq NP/poly [4, 25].

First, we show Theorem 5 (restated below), which implies that we cannot get similar kernelization results as Theorems 3 and 4 for planar graphs.

See 5

Proof.

We provide an OR-cross-composition from Linked Planar 3-SAT [37] based on Construction 2 that is used in the proof of Theorem 2. We say that two instances of Linked Planar 3-SAT are equivalent if the two formulas have the same number of variables and the same number of clauses. Assume we are given tt equivalent instances x1,x2,…,xtx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{t} of Linked Planar 3-SAT. We apply Construction 2 to each instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT. We identify the vertices r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} (the start positions of the main robots) of all instances. Then each edge incident with r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} we subdivide s+2=|X|+|Y|+2s+2=|X|+|Y|+2 times, where |X||X| and |Y||Y| are the number of variables and clauses, respectively. We set c=16⋅|X|+(s+2)⋅(|Y|+3)+1c=16\cdot|X|+(s+2)\cdot(|Y|+3)+1. This finishes the construction. For an illustration see Figure 14.

The edge subdivisions ensure that it is too expensive to move obnoxious robots between the instances. Intuitively, the allowed movement amount forces r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} to meet through one of the instances. The formal correctness is analogous to Lemmas 18 and 19. ∎

Next, we prove Theorem 6 (restated below), that is, we presumably cannot drop the parameter kk from the kernelization results in Theorems 3 and 4.

See 6

Proof.

We provide an OR-cross-composition from Linked Planar 3-SAT [37] based on Construction 3 that is used in the proof of Theorem 2. We say that two instances of Linked Planar 3-SAT are equivalent if the two formulas have the same number of variables and the same number of clauses. Assume we are given tt equivalent instances x1,x2,…,xtx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{t} of Linked Planar 3-SAT. We apply Construction 3 to each instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT with one small modification: we do not place any obnoxious robots in the variable gadgets. Note that the created instances all have the same horizontal size when embedded into a grid using the description on Lemma 20. We place the instances on top of each other (aligned) such that they to not overlap, see Figure 15 for an illustration. Then in each instance, the we subdivide the edges incident with r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, respectively, c+1c+1 times, where we specify cc later, respectively. We put a main robot on each newly created vertex. We embed the new vertices produced by the edge subdivisions horizontally to the left and right, respectively, from the original positions of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, respectively. Now we create a vertical path connecting all r1r_{1}-vertices of all instances and a vertical path connecting all r2r_{2}-vertices of all instances. We place main robots on all vertices of those two paths. For an illustration see Figure 15. Now, for each instance, we create one additional path with main robots on each vertex as follows. Let (x,y)(x,y) be the coordinates of the original grid point of the r1r_{1}-vertex of an instance (before the edge subdivisions). Then we start a path at grid point (x−1,y−1)(x-1,y-1) of length k′<c−1k^{\prime}<c-1 horizontally to the left, where we specify k′k^{\prime} later. Furthermore, we connect the vertex on grid point (x−1,y−1)(x-1,y-1) to the one on grid point (x−1,y)(x-1,y).

The intuition here is that instead of having two main robots meet from each side of an instance constructed by Construction 3, we create a connection between the main robots on the left side of the instances and the main robots on the right side of the instances by moving k′k^{\prime} robots into one of the instances. This is why the obnoxious robots in the variable gadgets are removed. The main robots will play the role of the obnoxious robots instead. This also means that k′k^{\prime} essentially needs to equal the number of steps made by main robots in the reduction of Theorem 2. Since the other paths on both sides of the instances have length c+1c+1, main robots on those paths cannot be moved, since broken connections cannot be repaired with less than cc moves.

To finish the construction, we set k′=12⋅|X|+6⋅|Y|+s+5k^{\prime}=12\cdot|X|+6\cdot|Y|+s+5, where |X||X| and |Y||Y| are the numbers of variables and clauses, respectively, and s=90⋅(|X|+|Y|)−4s=90\cdot(|X|+|Y|)-4. We set c=(k′)2+(s+2)⋅|Y|c=(k^{\prime})^{2}+(s+2)\cdot|Y|.

Note that for the main robots on the left and the right side of the instances to be connected, a connection through one of the instances has to be established. The formal correctness is analogous to Theorem 2 with a few minor differences: If one of the instances is a yes-instance, then we can move the main robots on the path of length k′k^{\prime} next to the instance through the instance using (k′)2(k^{\prime})^{2} moves. In the variable gadget, the main robots assume the role of the obnoxious robots in the original reduction, that is, they leave the same vertices in the variable gadgets unoccupied as the obnoxious robots, such that the obnoxious robots on the paths from clause gadgets to variable gadgets can move if the variable is set to a truth value that satisfied the corresponding literal of the clause. Those are (s+2)⋅|Y|(s+2)\cdot|Y| moves in total.

For the other direction, also analogous arguments hold with the following modification. We argue that the main robots cannot take “short-cuts” through paths connecting variable gadgets and clause gadgets since moving all obnoxious robots out of the way and moving main robots into the path costs at least 2⋅(s+2)22\cdot(s+2)^{2} moves. For large enough |X||X| and |Y||Y| we have that 2⋅(s+2)2>c2\cdot(s+2)^{2}>c, and hence this is not possible. It follows that we can use the same arguments for the correctness as in the proof of Theorem 2. ∎

Finally, we prove Theorem 7 (restated below), that is, we presumably cannot improve the kernel size from Theorem 4. For this kernelization lower bound, we use the weak cross-compositions framework [30, 25] to refute the existence of a polynomial kernel of a certain size for a parameterized problem under the assumption that coNP ⊈\not\subseteq NP/poly. A weak cross-composition of a problem L⊆{0,1}∗L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*} into a parameterized problem PP (with respect to a polynomial equivalence relation RR on the instances of LL) is an algorithm that takes tt RR-equivalent instances x1,…,xtx_{1},\ldots,x_{t} of LL and constructs in time polynomial in ∑i=1t|xi|\sum_{i=1}^{t}|x_{i}| an instance (y,k)(y,k) of PP such that

  1. 1.

    k≤(maxi∈[t]⁡|xi|)O⁡(1)⋅t1dk\leq(\max_{i\in[t]}|x_{i}|)^{O(1)}\cdot t^{\frac{1}{d}} for some d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}, and

  2. 2.

    (y,k)(y,k) is a yes-instance of PP if and only if there is an i∈[t]i\in[t] s.t. xix_{i} is a yes-instance of LL.

If an NP-hard problem LL weakly cross-composes into a parameterized problem PP, then PP does not admit a polynomial kernel of size O⁡(kd−ε)O(k^{d-\varepsilon}) for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, unless coNP ⊆\subseteq NP/poly [30, 25].

See 7

Proof.

We provide a weak cross-composition from Linked Planar 3-SAT [37] based on Construction 3 that is used in the proof of Theorem 2. We say that two instances of Linked Planar 3-SAT are equivalent if the two formulas have the same number of variables and the same number of clauses. Assume we are given tt equivalent instances x1,x2,…,xtx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{t} of Linked Planar 3-SAT. Furthermore, assume that t=t′\sqrt{t}=t^{\prime} for some t′∈ℕt^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N} (if not, we can copy some of the instances sufficiently many times). We apply Construction 3 to each instance of Linked Planar 3-SAT. We remove the main robots from vertices r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} of all instances. Then in each instance, the we subdivide the edges incident with r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, respectively, s+4=90⋅(|X|+|Y|)s+4=90\cdot(|X|+|Y|) times, where |X||X| and |Y||Y| are the number of variables and clauses, respectively. We use the embedding for the instances described in Lemma 20 and embed the new vertices produced by the edge subdivisions horizontally to the left and right, respectively, from the original positions of r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}, respectively.

Let xmax=maxi∈[t]⁡|xt|x_{\max}=\max_{i\in[t]}|x_{t}|. We arrange the tt instances in a (t×t)(\sqrt{t}\times\sqrt{t})-“super grid” where each cell has size (xmax+4)×(xmax+4)(x_{\max}+4)\times(x_{\max}+4) and place one of the instances into each super grid cell so that there are at least 2 empty rows / columns of grid cells between each instance and the boundaries of the super grid cells. For an illustration see Figure 16. Now we place two verices r1⋆r^{\star}_{1} and r2⋆r^{\star}_{2} at the bottom-left and top-right corner of the super grid, respectively, and place main robots on them.

We create paths from r1⋆r^{\star}_{1} horizontally (to the right) and vertically (to the top) of length t⋅(xmax+4)−1\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4)-1, that is, they reach just short of the bottom-right and top-left corner of the super grid. From the vertical path, we create horizontal paths (to the left) of length t⋅(xmax+4)−1\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4)-1 along the bottom (plus one grid cell up) of each super grid cell. We connect this path (via vertical paths up) to the r1r_{1}-vertex of each instance in each super grid cell that it traverses. Now we do an analogous construction from r2⋆r^{\star}_{2}. We create paths from r2⋆r^{\star}_{2} horizontally (to the left) and vertically (to the bottom) of length t⋅(xmax+4)−1\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4)-1, that is, they also reach just short of the bottom-right and top-left corner of the super grid and do not touch the paths starting at r1⋆r^{\star}_{1}. From the vertical path, we create horizontal paths (to the left) of length t⋅(xmax+4)−1\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4)-1 along the top (minus one grid cell up) of each super grid cell. We connect this path (via vertical paths down) to the r2r_{2}-vertex of each instance in each super grid cell that it traverses. The path just described are depicted in red in Figure 16.

We set c=2⋅t⋅(xmax+4)+2⋅(s+4)+c′c=2\cdot\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4)+2\cdot(s+4)+c^{\prime}, where c′c^{\prime} is the allowed movement amout of an instance xix_{i} with i∈[t]i\in[t] (note that since the instances are equivalent, they all have the same allowed movement amount). This finishes the construction.

Note that for the main robots on r1⋆r^{\star}_{1} and r2⋆r^{\star}_{2}, respectively, to meet, they have to traverse at least one of the instances. Assume w.l.o.g. that the two robots meet in an instance (if they do not, we can move the meeting point to r1r_{1} or r2r_{2} with a respective neighbor of one of the instances). In order to reach said instance, the have to travel at least 2⋅t⋅(xmax+4)2\cdot\sqrt{t}\cdot(x_{\max}+4) along red paths in Figure 16. Furthermore, they have to traverse the edge-subdivision after r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} of said instance, which takes another 2⋅(s+4)2\cdot(s+4) steps. There are now c′c^{\prime} steps remaining to traverse at least one instance. The edge subdivisions ensure that it is too expensive to move obnoxious robots between the instances. Intuitively, the allowed movement amount forces r1r_{1} and r2r_{2} to meet through one of the instances. The formal correctness is analogous to Theorem 2. ∎

6 Collision Free Movement on Planar Graphs

In this section, we prove Theorem 8 (restated below), that is, we show that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k+ck+c if the input graph is planar.

See 8

To prove Theorem 8, we show that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is expressable in monadic second-order logic (MSO). This allows us to employ Courcelle’s famous theorem [2, 5, 6] to obtain the result.

We begin by recalling some basic notation and terminology for relational structures. A relational vocabulary is a finite set τ\tau of relation symbols, each of which is associated with a natural number, known as its arity. Given any relational vocabulary τ\tau, a τ\tau-structure is a pair 𝒜=(A,{R𝒜∣R∈τ})\mathcal{A}=(A,\{R^{\mathcal{A}}\mid R\in\tau\}); AA is said to be the universe of 𝒜\mathcal{A} while, for each R∈τR\in\tau, the interpretation R𝒜R^{\mathcal{A}} of RR in 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a subset of ArA^{r}, where rr is the arity of RR. Here, we are interested only in relational structures with finite universes, and where the maximum arity of any relation is two.

For any vocabulary τ\tau, the set of first-order formulas is built up from a countably infinite set of individual variables x1,x2,…x_{1},x_{2},\ldots, the relation symbols R∈τR\in\tau, the connectives ∧,∨,¬\wedge,\vee,\neg and the quantifiers ∀x,∃x\forall x,\exists x ranging over elements of the universe of the structure (for notational convenience we will also use standard shorthand such as ⇒\Rightarrow, ⇔\Leftrightarrow, ==, and ∈\in). Monadic second-order logic (MSO) additionally allows quantification over subsets of the universe via unary relation variables (which we will call set variables). Given an MSO-formula ϕ\phi, an individual variable xx (respectively a unary relation variable XX) appearing in ϕ\phi is said to be a free variable if xx (respectively XX) is not in the scope of a quantifier ∃x\exists x or ∀x\forall x (respectively ∃X\exists X or ∀X\forall X). We write ϕ⁡(X1,…,Xn,x1,…,xm)\phi(X_{1},\dots,X_{n},x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}) for a formula ψ\psi with with free relation variables X1,…,XnX_{1},\ldots,X_{n} and individual variables x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m}. Given subsets A1,…,An⊆AA_{1},\dots,A_{n}\subseteq A (formally these define interpretations of unary relation variables over AA) and elements a1,…,am∈Aa_{1},\dots,a_{m}\in A, we write 𝒜⊧ϕ⁡(A1,…,An,a1,…,am)\mathcal{A}\models\phi(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n},a_{1},\ldots,a_{m}) to mean that 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies ϕ\phi if the variables X1,…,Xn,x1,…,xmX_{1},\ldots,X_{n},x_{1},\ldots,x_{m} are interpreted as A1,…,An,a1,…,amA_{1},\ldots,A_{n},a_{1},\ldots,a_{m} respectively.

A tree decomposition of a τ\tau-structure 𝒜\mathcal{A} with universe AA is a pair (T,ℬ)(T,\mathcal{B}), where T=(VT,ET)T=(V_{T},E_{T}) is a tree and ℬ=(Bv)v∈VT\mathcal{B}=(B_{v})_{v\in V_{T}} is a collection of subsets of AA such that:

  1. 1.

    for all a∈Aa\in A, the set {v∈VT:a∈Bv}\{v\in V_{T}:a\in B_{v}\} is non-empty and induces a connected subtree in TT, and

  2. 2.

    for every relation symbol R∈τR\in\tau and every tuple (a1,…,ar)∈R𝒜(a_{1},\dots,a_{r})\in R^{\mathcal{A}}, there exists Bv∈ℬB_{v}\in\mathcal{B} such that a1,…,ar∈BVa_{1},\dots,a_{r}\in B_{V}.

As for graphs, the width of the tree decomposition (T,ℬ)(T,\mathcal{B}) is maxBv∈ℬ⁡|Bv|−1\max_{B_{v}\in\mathcal{B}}|B_{v}|-1, and the treewidth of 𝒜\mathcal{A} (denoted tw⁡(𝒜)\tw(\mathcal{A})) is the minimum width over all tree decompositions of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

We now give the formal definition of the MSO Model Checking problem.

MSO Model Checking Input: A relational structure 𝒜\mathcal{A} and an MSO-formula ϕ\phi. Question: Are there subsets A1,…,An⊆AA_{1},\dots,A_{n}\subseteq A and elements a1,…,am∈Aa_{1},\dots,a_{m}\in A such that 𝒜⊧ϕ⁡(A1,…,An,a1,…,am)\mathcal{A}\models\phi(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n},a_{1},\ldots,a_{m})?

Courcelle’s theorem [2, 5, 6] implies the following.

Theorem 23 ([2, 5, 6]).

MSO Model Checking is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by tw⁡(𝒜)+|ϕ|\tw(\mathcal{A})+|\phi|.

We begin by defining the relational structure 𝒜\mathcal{A} that will encode our instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. Assume we are given an instance (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. The universe AA of 𝒜\mathcal{A} consists of the following elements:

  • •

    The set VV of vertices.

  • •

    The set EE of edges.

  • •

    The set [c][c] of steps.

  • •

    The set Sv=V×[c]S_{v}=V\times[c] of vertex-step pairs.

  • •

    The set Se=V×[c]S_{e}=V\times[c] of edge-step pairs.

The structure 𝒜\mathcal{A} has eight relation symbols (two unary and six binary relations), with the following interpretations:

  • •

    The unary relation main\main on VV, where main⁡(v)⇔v∈R\main(v)\Leftrightarrow v\in R.

  • •

    The unary relation robot\robot on VV, where robot⁡(v)⇔v∈R∪O\robot(v)\Leftrightarrow v\in R\cup O.

  • •

    The binary relation inc\inc on V×EV\times E, where inc⁡(v,e)⇔v∈e\inc(v,e)\Leftrightarrow v\in e.

  • •

    The binary relation vertex\vertex on Sv×VS_{v}\times V, where vertex⁡((v,i),w)⇔v=w\vertex((v,i),w)\Leftrightarrow v=w.

  • •

    The binary relation edge\edge on Se×ES_{e}\times E, where edge⁡((e,i),f)⇔e=f\edge((e,i),f)\Leftrightarrow e=f.

  • •

    The binary relation stepv\step_{v} on Sv×[c]S_{v}\times[c], where stepv⁡((v,i),j)⇔i=j\step_{v}((v,i),j)\Leftrightarrow i=j.

  • •

    The binary relation stepe\step_{e} on Se×[c]S_{e}\times[c], where stepe⁡((e,i),j)⇔i=j\step_{e}((e,i),j)\Leftrightarrow i=j.

  • •

    The binary relation nextstep\nextstep on [c]×[c][c]\times[c], where nextstep⁡(i,j)⇔i=j+1\nextstep(i,j)\Leftrightarrow i=j+1.

We now bound the treewidth of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Let (T,ℬ)(T,\mathcal{B}) be a tree decomposition for GG of width tw⁡(G)\tw(G). We construct a tree decomposition (T,ℬ′)(T,\mathcal{B}^{\prime}) for 𝒜\mathcal{A}, indexed by the same tree T=(VT,ET)T=(V_{T},E_{T}), as follows. Fix a vertex v∈VTv\in V_{T}, and let BvB_{v} be the corresponding element of ℬ\mathcal{B}. We define the corresponding element of ℬ′\mathcal{B}^{\prime} to be

Bv′:=Bv∪{e={u,w}∈E:v,w∈Bv}∪{s=(u,i)∈Sv:u∈Bv}∪{s=({u,w},i)∈Se:u,w∈Bv}∪[c].B_{v}^{\prime}:=B_{v}\cup\{e=\{u,w\}\in E:v,w\in B_{v}\}\cup\{s=(u,i)\in S_{v}:u\in B_{v}\}\cup\{s=(\{u,w\},i)\in S_{e}:u,w\in B_{v}\}\cup[c].

It is straightforward to verify that, with this definition, (T,ℬ′)(T,\mathcal{B}^{\prime}) is indeed a tree decomposition for 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Furthermore, it is immediate that |Bv′|≤|Bv|+(|Bv|2)+c⋅(|Bv|2)+c⋅|Bv|+c|B_{v}^{\prime}|\leq|B_{v}|+\binom{|B_{v}|}{2}+c\cdot\binom{|B_{v}|}{2}+c\cdot|B_{v}|+c. Hence, we have the following.

Lemma 24.

It holds that tw⁡(𝒜)∈O⁡(c⋅tw⁡(G)2)\tw(\mathcal{A})\in O(c\cdot\tw(G)^{2}).

We now proceed to define the formula ϕ\phi. The main idea (intuitively) is as follows.

  • •

    For each main robot, we try to find a movement of length cc.

  • •

    If an obnoxious robot is encountered in a movement, then we try to find a (non-trivial) movement of length cc for the obnoxious robot.

  • •

    We know that in total, we can only have cc non-trivial movements in the movement plan.

  • •

    The movement plan should be collision-free and the end-configuration of the main robots should induce a subgraph with property Π\Pi.

  • •

    The length of the moment plan should be at most cc.

We introduce several subformulas:

  • •

    movement⁡(X)\operatorname{movement}(X) has as free variable XX and checks whether these are exactly cc elements from SvS_{v} that correspond to a movement.

    movement⁡(X)=\displaystyle\operatorname{movement}(X)=\ ∃x1,…,xc∈Sv​(⋀i∈[c](xi∈X∧stepv⁡(x,i))∧∀x∈X​⋁i∈[c](x=xi)∧CLOSE\displaystyle\exists x_{1},\ldots,x_{c}\in S_{v}\Big(\bigwedge_{i\in[c]}(x_{i}\in X\wedge\step_{v}(x,i))\wedge\forall x\in X\bigvee_{i\in[c]}(x=x_{i})\wedge
    ⋀i∈[c−1](∃v∈V⁡(vertex⁡(xi,v)∧vertex⁡(xi+1,v))∨CLOSE\displaystyle\bigwedge_{i\in[c-1]}(\exists v\in V(\vertex(x_{i},v)\wedge\vertex(x_{i+1},v))\vee
    ∃e∈E​∃v,w∈V⁡(inc⁡(v,e)∧inc⁡(w,e)∧vertex⁡(xi,v)∧vertex⁡(xi+1,w))\displaystyle\exists e\in E\ \exists v,w\in V(\inc(v,e)\wedge\inc(w,e)\wedge\vertex(x_{i},v)\wedge\vertex(x_{i+1},w)\Big)

    Note that the size of movement⁡(X)\operatorname{movement}(X) is in O⁡(c)O(c). The formula checks whether there are cc elements in SvS_{v} with cc different steps (note that this implies that the elements are different) and that each element in XX is equal to one of these cc elements from SvS_{v}. This implies that XX contains exactly cc elements from SvS_{v}. Then the formula checks for every pair of vertex-step pairs in XX with consecutive time steps whether they have the same vertex or adjacent vertices.

  • •

    collision−free⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{1},X_{2}) has as free variables X1X_{1} and X2X_{2}, which are expected to be movements, and checks whether they are collision-free.

    collision−free⁡(X1,X2)=\displaystyle\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{1},X_{2})=\ ∀x1∈X1​∀x2∈X2​∀i∈[c]​∃v,w∈V⁡((stepv⁡(x1,i)∧step⁡(x2,i))⇒CLOSE\displaystyle\forall x_{1}\in X_{1}\ \forall x_{2}\in X_{2}\ \forall i\in[c]\ \exists v,w\in V\Big((\step_{v}(x_{1},i)\wedge\step(x_{2},i))\Rightarrow
    (v≠w∧vertex⁡(x1,v)∧vertex⁡(x2,w))∧\displaystyle(v\neq w\wedge\vertex(x_{1},v)\wedge\vertex(x_{2},w)\Big)\wedge
    ∀x1,x2∈X1​∀x3,x4∈X2​∀i,j∈[c]​∀v,w∈V⁡((nextstep⁡(i,j)∧CLOSECLOSE\displaystyle\forall x_{1},x_{2}\in X_{1}\ \forall x_{3},x_{4}\in X_{2}\ \forall i,j\in[c]\ \forall v,w\in V\Big((\nextstep(i,j)\wedge
    OPENstepv⁡(x1,i)∧step⁡(x2,j)∧stepv⁡(x3,i)∧step⁡(x4,j))⇒\displaystyle\step_{v}(x_{1},i)\wedge\step(x_{2},j)\wedge\step_{v}(x_{3},i)\wedge\step(x_{4},j))\Rightarrow
    OPEN¬(vertex⁡(x1,v)∧vertex⁡(x2,w)∧vertex⁡(x3,w)∧vertex⁡(x4,v)))\displaystyle\neg(\vertex(x_{1},v)\wedge\vertex(x_{2},w)\wedge\vertex(x_{3},w)\wedge\vertex(x_{4},v))\Big)

    Note that the size of collision−free⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{1},X_{2}) is constant.

  • •

    move⁡(X,x)\operatorname{move}(X,x) has as free variables XX and xx where XX is expected to be a movement and xx is expected to be an element from SeS_{e}. It checks whether the edge-step pair x=(e,i)x=(e,i) is a move in the movement, that is, whether at step ii there is a move along edge ee in the movement XX.

    move⁡(X,x)=\displaystyle\operatorname{move}(X,x)=\ ∃x1,x2∈X​∃v,w∈V​∃e∈E​∃i,j∈[c]​(nextstep⁡(i,j)∧stepv⁡(x1,i)∧stepv⁡(x2,j)∧CLOSE\displaystyle\exists x_{1},x_{2}\in X\ \exists v,w\in V\ \exists e\in E\ \exists i,j\in[c]\Big(\nextstep(i,j)\wedge\step_{v}(x_{1},i)\wedge\step_{v}(x_{2},j)\wedge
    OPENv≠w∧vertex⁡(x1,v)∧vertex⁡(x2,w)∧inc⁡(v,e)∧inc⁡(w,e)∧edge⁡(x,e)∧stepe⁡(x,i))\displaystyle v\neq w\wedge\vertex(x_{1},v)\wedge\vertex(x_{2},w)\wedge\inc(v,e)\wedge\inc(w,e)\wedge\edge(x,e)\wedge\step_{e}(x,i)\Big)

    Note that the size of move⁡(X,x)\operatorname{move}(X,x) is constant.

  • •

    start⁡(X,x)\operatorname{start}(X,x), end⁡(X,x)\operatorname{end}(X,x), and visit⁡(X,x)\operatorname{visit}(X,x) have as free variables XX and xx, respectively, where XX is expected to be a movement and xx is expected to be an element from VV. start⁡(X,x)\operatorname{start}(X,x) checks whether the movement XX starts at vertex xx. end⁡(X,x)\operatorname{end}(X,x) checks whether the movement XX ends at vertex xx. visit⁡(X,x)\operatorname{visit}(X,x) checks whether the movement XX visits vertex xx at some step.

    start⁡(X,x)=∃x1∈X⁡(vertex⁡(x1,x)∧stepv⁡(x,1))\displaystyle\operatorname{start}(X,x)=\exists x_{1}\in X(\vertex(x_{1},x)\wedge\step_{v}(x,1))
    end⁡(X,x)=∃x1∈X⁡(vertex⁡(x1,x)∧stepv⁡(x,c))\displaystyle\operatorname{end}(X,x)=\exists x_{1}\in X(\vertex(x_{1},x)\wedge\step_{v}(x,c))
    visit⁡(X,x)=∃x1∈X⁡(vertex⁡(x1,x))\displaystyle\operatorname{visit}(X,x)=\exists x_{1}\in X(\vertex(x_{1},x))

    Note that the sizes of start⁡(X,x)\operatorname{start}(X,x), end⁡(X,x)\operatorname{end}(X,x), and visit⁡(X,x)\operatorname{visit}(X,x) are each constant.

Now we are ready to give the formula ϕ\phi. Denote with c⋆=min⁡(k+ℓ,c)c^{\star}=\min(k+\ell,c).

ϕ⁡(X1,…,Xc⋆,x1,…,xc)=\displaystyle\phi(X_{1},\ldots,X_{c^{\star}},x_{1},\ldots,x_{c})= ⋀i∈[c⋆]movement⁡(Xi)∧⋀i,j∈[c⋆]((i≠j)⇒collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj))∧\displaystyle\bigwedge_{i\in[c^{\star}]}\operatorname{movement}(X_{i})\wedge\bigwedge_{i,j\in[c^{\star}]}((i\neq j)\Rightarrow\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}))\wedge
∀v∈V⁡((robot⁡(v)∧(⋁i∈[c⋆]visit⁡(Xi,v)))⇒(⋁i∈[c⋆]start⁡(Xi,v)))∧\displaystyle\forall v\in V\Big((\robot(v)\wedge(\bigvee_{i\in[c^{\star}]}\operatorname{visit}(X_{i},v)))\Rightarrow(\bigvee_{i\in[c^{\star}]}\operatorname{start}(X_{i},v))\Big)\wedge
∀x∈Se​((⋁i∈[c⋆]move⁡(Xi,x))⇒(⋁i∈[c](x=xi)))∧\displaystyle\forall x\in S_{e}\Big((\bigvee_{i\in[c^{\star}]}\operatorname{move}(X_{i},x))\Rightarrow(\bigvee_{i\in[c]}(x=x_{i}))\Big)\wedge
∃X⊆V((∀v∈V((main(v)∧⋀i∈[c⋆]¬start(Xi,v))∨\displaystyle\exists X\subseteq V\Big((\forall v\in V((\main(v)\wedge\bigwedge_{i\in[c^{\star}]}\neg\operatorname{start}(X_{i},v))\vee
OPENOPEN∃w∈V⁡(main⁡(w)∧(⋁i∈[c⋆](start⁡(Xi,w)∧end⁡(Xi,v)))⇔(v∈X)))∧Π⁡(X))\displaystyle\exists w\in V(\main(w)\wedge(\bigvee_{i\in[c^{\star}]}(\operatorname{start}(X_{i},w)\wedge\operatorname{end}(X_{i},v)))\Leftrightarrow(v\in X)))\wedge\Pi(X)\Big)

Note that the size of the formula ϕ\phi is in O⁡(c2+|Π|)O(c^{2}+|\Pi|). Since the graph property Π\Pi is recursively enumerable, we can conclude |Π⁡(X)|=f⁡(k)|\Pi(X)|=f(k) for |X|=k|X|=k and some computable function ff. Hence, we have the following.

Lemma 25.

It holds that |ϕ|∈O⁡(c2)+f⁡(k)|\phi|\in O(c^{2})+f(k), for some computable function ff.

It remains to show that the formula is correct.

Lemma 26.

The formula ϕ\phi is satisfiable if and only if (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi.

Proof.

First, assume that ϕ\phi is satisfiable. We show that then (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. Let X1,…,Xc⋆,x1,…,xcX_{1},\ldots,X_{c^{\star}},x_{1},\ldots,x_{c} denote a satisfying assignment for ϕ\phi. We construct a movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} as follows. We have that the sets XiX_{i} with i∈[c⋆]i\in[c^{\star}] satisfy movement⁡(Xi)\operatorname{movement}(X_{i}). It follows that Xi={(v1,1),(v2,2),…,(vc,c)}X_{i}=\{(v_{1},1),(v_{2},2),\ldots,(v_{c},c)\} (see the first line of the definition of movement⁡(X)\operatorname{movement}(X)). We claim that Mi=(v1,v2,…,vc)M_{i}=(v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{c}) is a movement. The second and third line of the definition of movement⁡(X)\operatorname{movement}(X) give us exactly that for all vj,vj+1v_{j},v_{j+1} with j∈[c−1]j\in[c-1] we have that vj=vj+1v_{j}=v_{j+1} or {vj,vj+1}∈E\{v_{j},v_{j+1}\}\in E. Hence, we can conclude that MiM_{i} is a movement. Now for each MiM_{i} that is a movement for a robot r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O, we add MiM_{i} to the movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M}. For each r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O such that none of the MiM_{i} with i∈[c⋆]i\in[c^{\star}] is a movement for rr, we add a trivial movement to the movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M}. Now we show the following, from which clearly follows that (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi.

  1. 1.

    For each r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O there is at most one i∈[c⋆]i\in[c^{\star}] such that MiM_{i} is a movement for ii, that is, the movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} is well-defined.

  2. 2.

    The movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} is collision-free.

  3. 3.

    len⁡(ℳ)≤c\len(\mathcal{M})\leq c and G​[R⋆​(ℳ)]∈ΠG[R^{\star}(\mathcal{M})]\in\Pi.

Consider the first statement and assume for contradiction that there are two movements MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} with i≠ji\neq j for some r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O. Note that in ϕ\phi, the subformula collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}) is checked and evaluates to true, since otherwise ϕ\phi would evaluate to false. In collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}) it is, in particular, checked, that (v1,1)∈Xi(v_{1},1)\in X_{i} and (v1′,1)∈Xj(v^{\prime}_{1},1)\in X_{j} implies v1≠v1′v_{1}\neq v^{\prime}_{1}. It follows that MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} cannot both be a movement for the same r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O.

Consider the second statement and assume for contradiction that there are two movements MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} with i≠ji\neq j for robots r,r′∈R∪Or,r^{\prime}\in R\cup O, respectively, that are not collision-free. First, consider that both MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} are non-trivial. Then in ϕ\phi, the subformula collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}) is checked and evaluates to true, since otherwise ϕ\phi would evaluate to false. However, if MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} then there exists some vertex vv and some step tt such that both rr and r′r^{\prime} occupy vv in step tt or there exit an edge {v,w}∈E\{v,w\}\in E and some step tt such that rr occupies vv in step tt and ww in step t+1t+1 and r′r^{\prime} occupies ww in step tt and vv in step t+1t+1. In this case we can verify that collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}) evaluates to false: In the former case the first two lines in the definition of collision−free⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{1},X_{2}) evaluate to false, and in the latter case, the last three lines in the definition of collision−free⁡(X1,X2)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{1},X_{2}) evaluate to false. In each case we reach a contradiction. Now consider the case that w.l.o.g. MiM_{i} is a non-trivial movement and MjM_{j} is a trivial movement. If MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} are not collision-free, then there must be a step tt such that robot rr occupies r′r^{\prime} in step tt. However, then robot⁡(r′)\robot(r^{\prime}) and visit⁡(Xi,r′)\operatorname{visit}(X_{i},r^{\prime}) both evaluate to true. It follows that ⋁j∈[c⋆]start⁡(Xj,r′)\bigvee_{j\in[c^{\star}]}\operatorname{start}(X_{j},r^{\prime}) must also evaluate to true. It follows that MjM_{j} corresponds to some XjX_{j} and collision−free⁡(Xi,Xj)\operatorname{collision-free}(X_{i},X_{j}) evaluates to true. By the same arguments as earlier we can conclude that MiM_{i} and MjM_{j} are collision-free.

Finally, consider the third statement. Let MiM_{i} be a non-trivial movement for some r∈R∪Or\in R\cup O. First, it is straightforward to verify that if robot rr moves along edge {v,w}\{v,w\} in step tt, then move⁡(Xi,({v,w},t))\operatorname{move}(X_{i},(\{v,w\},t)) evaluates to true. Since the movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} is collision-free according to the previous arguments, we have that for a fixed ({v,w},t)(\{v,w\},t), the subformula move⁡(Xi,({v,w},t))\operatorname{move}(X_{i},(\{v,w\},t)) evaluates to true for at most one XiX_{i}. In the third line of the definition of ϕ\phi it is checked that whenever move⁡(Xi,({v,w},t))\operatorname{move}(X_{i},(\{v,w\},t)) evaluates to true, then ({v,w},t)=xj(\{v,w\},t)=x_{j} for some j∈[c]j\in[c]. It follows that the set {x1,x2,…,xc}\{x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{c}\} contains all moves made by robots according to movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M}. It follows that there are at most cc different moves, and hence len⁡(ℳ)≤c\len(\mathcal{M})\leq c. Next, consider the last two lines of the definition of ϕ\phi. We show that the set XX here corresponds to R⋆​(ℳ)R^{\star}(\mathcal{M}): The formula ensures that a vertex vv is contained in XX if and only if vv is a main robot and not the start of any XiX_{i} (in this case vv has a trivial movement), or there is a main robot ww and an XiX_{i} starting with ww that ends in vv, that is, XiX_{i} corresponds to a movement for a main robot ww that ends in vv. Finally ϕ\phi checks whether Π⁡(X)\Pi(X) evaluates to true. It follows that G​[R⋆​(ℳ)]∈ΠG[R^{\star}(\mathcal{M})]\in\Pi.

Now assume that (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) is a yes-instance of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi. Then there is a collision-free movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} that contains at most c⋆c^{\star} non-trivial movements which make at most cc moves. Let X1,X2,…,Xc⋆X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{c^{\star}} correspond to the non-trivial movements (if there are strictly less than c⋆c^{\star} non-trivial movements, we can add sets XX that only contain a vertex that is never visited (we can easily ensure that such a vertex always exists). Let x1,x2,…,xcx_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{c} correspond to the moves. If there are strictly less than cc moves, then we can duplicate arbitrary moves. By analogous arguments to the first part of this proof, we can argue that ϕ⁡(X1,X2,…,Xc⋆,x1,x2,…,xc)\phi(X_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{c^{\star}},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{c}) evaluates to true. ∎

Now we have all ingredients to prove Theorem 8.

Proof of Theorem 8.

Given an instance (G=(V,E),R,O,c)(G=(V,E),R,O,c) of Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi, we first apply Reduction Rule 1. By Lemma 21 this creates an equivalent instance (G′=(V′,E′),R,O′,c)(G^{\prime}=(V^{\prime},E^{\prime}),R,O^{\prime},c). We can observe that diam⁡(G′)∈O⁡(k⋅c)\diam(G^{\prime})\in O(k\cdot c) (where if G′G^{\prime} is disconnected, we assume that diam⁡(G′)\diam(G^{\prime}) is the maximum diameter of the connected components of G′G^{\prime}). This follows from the fact that after Reduction Rule 1 is applied, every vertex in G′G^{\prime} has distance at most cc from some r∈Rr\in R, and for every r,r′∈Rr,r^{\prime}\in R such that rr and r′r^{\prime} are in the same connected component of G′G^{\prime}, we have that dist⁡(r,r′)∈O⁡(k⋅c)\dist(r,r^{\prime})\in O(k\cdot c). Since G′G^{\prime} is planar, it is well-known that this implies that tw⁡(G′)∈O⁡(k⋅c)\tw(G^{\prime})\in O(k\cdot c). Theorem 8 now follows from Lemmas 26, 24 and 25, and Theorem 23. ∎

We remark that the described algorithm does not exploit planarity. It is only used to upper-bound the treewidth with the diameter of the input graph. Hence, the algorithm also implies that Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k+ck+c and the treewidth of the input graph combined.

7 Collision Free Movement on Unit Disk Graphs

In this section, we consider the canonical optimization version of the problem Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity, where the objective is to minimize the length of the movement plan. We prove Theorem 9 (restated below), that is, we give a fixed-parameter approximation algorithm for Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity parameterized by k+ck+c on unit disk graphs, that produces a solution with energy at most 2⋅OPT+3​k2\cdot\text{OPT}+3k, where OPT is the energy of an optimal solution (Theorem 9). Here, the parameter cc is the number of moves in an optimal solution. In fact, the algorithm we present also works on a slightly more general graph class, so-called clique grids, which are generalizations of grids and defined as follows.

Definition 27 (Clique Grid) ([24]).

A graph G=(V,E)G=(V,E) is a clique grid graph if there exists a function f:V→[t]×[t′]f:V\rightarrow[t]\times[t^{\prime}] for some t,t′∈ℕt,t^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N} such that

  • •

    for all (i,j)∈[t]×[t′](i,j)\in[t]\times[t^{\prime}] it holds that f−1​(i,j)f^{-1}(i,j) is a clique in GG, and

  • •

    for all {u,v}∈E\{u,v\}\in E it holds that if f⁡(u)=(i,j)f(u)=(i,j) and f⁡(v)=(i′,j′)f(v)=(i^{\prime},j^{\prime}), then |i−i′|≤2|i-i^{\prime}|\leq 2 and |j−j′|≤2|j-j^{\prime}|\leq 2.

The function ff is a representation of GG.

It is known that unit disk graphs are clique grids and that, given the point set of the unit disk graph, a representation can be computed in polynomial time.

Lemma 28 ([24]).

Let GG be a unit disk graph with point set DD. Then GG is a clique grid graph and a representation ff of GG can be computed from DD in polynomial time.

In this section, we will assume that a representation of the input graph in form of a point set or a clique grid representation is given as part of the input. Now we prove the following result.

See 9

We present an algorithm to prove Theorem 9 with the following steps. Assume we are given an instance (G=(V,E),R,O)(G=(V,E),R,O) of (the optimization version) of Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity and we have a clique grid representation of GG. We first start with some basic “guessing” steps, which in this context means that we exhaustively enumerate and check all possibilities for the guess.

  • •

    We first guess the optimal value for cc.

  • •

    We exhaustively apply Reduction Rule 1, that is, we remove each vertex that has distance more than cc from every main robot.

  • •

    We guess a tree TT with kk vertices that witnesses the connectivity in an optimal solution of the instance.

  • •

    We guess a bijection between the main robots and the vertices of TT.

Next, we define a continuation type ti​(v)t_{i}(v) of a vertex vv for step ii and we defines a type of a vertex vv as follows:

  • •

    For step cc, the continuation type tc​(v)t_{c}(v) of vertex vv is an element from {F,O,r1,r2,…,rk}\{F,O,r_{1},r_{2},\ldots,r_{k}\} and set as follows. We set tc​(v)=Ft_{c}(v)=F meaning the vertex is free if v∉O∪Rv\notin O\cup R, we set tc​(v)=Ot_{c}(v)=O meaning the vertex is occupied by an obnoxious robot if v∈Ov\in O, and we set tc​(v)=rit_{c}(v)=r_{i} meaning the vertex is occupied by a main robot if v=ri∈Rv=r_{i}\in R.

  • •

    For step i<ci<c, the continuation type ti​(v)t_{i}(v) of a vertex vv is defined as the following set:

    For each clique CC that is neighboring the clique of ii, and each v′v^{\prime} that is a neighbor of cc in CC, add the pair (C,ti+1​(v′))(C,t_{i+1}(v^{\prime})) to ti​(v)t_{i}(v).

  • •

    The type of vv is a triple consisting of the clique CC of vv, an element from {F,O,r1,…,rk}\{F,O,r_{1},\ldots,r_{k}\} indicating whether vv is free or occupied (as above), and the list of all continuation types of vv for all steps i≤ci\leq c.

  • •

    If there is a vertex type such that there are at most 2​k+c+22k+c+2 vertices of that type, we additionally add the identity of the vertices to their type.

Note that since we apply Reduction Rule 1, we have O⁡(k⋅c2)O(k\cdot c^{2}) different cliques (this follows from an analogous argument as the proof of Theorem 3). Since each clique only has constantly many neighboring cliques, the number of different continuation types is in 2O⁡(k⋅c2)2^{O(k\cdot c^{2})}. We can iteratively compute the continuation types of all vertices for all steps in 2O⁡(k⋅c2)⋅nO⁡(1)2^{O(k\cdot c^{2})}\cdot n^{O(1)} time, starting with step cc, in a straightforward way.

The intuition behind the continuation types is as follows. If a robot arrives at a vertex in step cc it cannot travel any further afterwards. So the only relevant information is whether the vertex is free or occupied by another robot. In the latter case, the other robot needs to be moved before step cc to avoid a collision. If a robot arrives at a vertex at some step i<ci<c, it can travel further, so it is relevant which types of vertices it can reach. This is encoded in the list of clique-vertex type pairs. Of course, it is also still relevant whether the vertex is free or occupied by another robot. Note that if a clique-neighbor type pair is in the list of the type of a vertex, it only means that the vertex can reach some neighbor in the clique with the type (not all). This, intuitively, is the reason for the approximation factor two, since we can only guarantee that we move a robot to a vertex of the “correct” vertex type in the “correct” clique at each step, but we cannot guarantee that we move the robot to the “correct” vertex. So the solution we construct may need an extra step in each clique to move to the “correct” vertex.

The algorithm now continues with a second guessing step, where we guess up to max⁡{c,k}\max\{c,k\} vectors MiM_{i} of vertex types that each have length up to cc (possibly including duplicates). Whenever there is a type switch from one position to the next in the vector, we consider this to be a move. We reject all guesses where the total number of moves is greater than cc. These vectors will be templates for the movements in the movement plan we construct. In a later step, we will replace the types with actual vertices. The main goal is to first move the main robots into the “correct” cliques, and then afterwards to the “correct” vertices inside the cliques. For a given guess, we make the following checks:

  • •

    For each vector MiM_{i}, we check whether it is a movement. More specifically, whenever two subsequent entries in the vector are two different types t,t′t,t^{\prime} we check whether the types are neighboring types, that is, whether there are two vertices u,vu,v which are neighbors and uu has type tt, and vv has type t′t^{\prime}. Furthermore, we check whether the first entry of the vector is a vertex type for a vertex that is occupied by a robot.

  • •

    For each vector MiM_{i}, we check whether it is collision-free, that is, whenever there is a vertex type tt in the vector for a vertex that is occupied by a robot, there is another movement vector MjM_{j} starting with type tt that moves the robot away (sufficiently early).

    If several vectors (say ℓ\ell) move a robot to a vertex of type tt for a vertex that is occupied by another robot, such that the time steps where the moved robots occupy the vertex of type tt intersect, we check whether there are ℓ\ell other movements vector starting with type tt that move the robots away (sufficiently early).

  • •

    For each pair of vectors Mi,MjM_{i},M_{j} we check whether they are collision-free. This is only relevant if the vectors contain types that have vertex identities.

  • •

    We want to find vectors where the number of moves in each step is minimum, that is, moves only happen simultaneously if they have to, that is, when robots move around a cycle of length at least 3.

    We check whether at each step across all vectors, there is either at most one move, or at most one cyclic set of moves.

If none of the above checks fail, we check whether TT is a subgraph of GG such that the location of the vertices of TT in GG complies with our guess, that is, they have the correct type. To do this, we use a subgraph finding algorithm that allows us to define a cost function for possible mappings from the vertices of TT to the vertices of GG. We use this to make sure that the subgraph embedding complies with our guesses.

Theorem 29 ([12]).

Let FF be an undirected graph with ss vertices and treewidth tt. Let GG be an undirected graph with nn vertices and let c:V⁡(F)×V⁡(G)→ℕc:V(F)\times V(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{N} be a cost function of mapping a vertex of FF to a vertex of GG. If FF is a subgraph of GG, then it is possible to find in time 2O⁡(s)⋅nO⁡(t)2^{O(s)}\cdot n^{O(t)} a subgraph embedding ϕ\phi that minimizes c⁡(ϕ)c(\phi).

We define a cost function cc as follows: For v∈V⁡(T)v\in V(T) such that we guessed that vv is mapped to main robot rr, and the movement for rr moves the robot to a vertex of type tt, and v′∈V⁡(G)v^{\prime}\in V(G), we set

c⁡(v,v′)={1, if ​v′​ has type ​t,n, otherwise.c(v,v^{\prime})=\begin{cases}1,&\text{ if }v^{\prime}\text{ has type }t,\\ n,&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

We use the algorithm behind Theorem 29 to find subgraph embedding ϕ\phi for TT into GG of minimal cost. If the cost is larger than kk, we reject the guess.

Now we have all ingredients to construct a movement plan ℳ\mathcal{M} for the Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity instance. For each movement M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M} we have that the first vertex type for a vertex that is occupied by a robot, otherwise the checks described above fail. We pick an arbitrary vertex of that type (a different one for each movement) and identify the robot on that vertex as the one corresponding to the movement. We iterate through the steps from i=1i=1 to cc:

  • •

    We perform the iith move of each move of each movement. That is, for each M∈ℳM\in\mathcal{M}, we pick a (different) vertex vv of type M⁡[i+1]M[i+1], and move the robot corresponding to MM from its previous position to vv.

    When picking the vertices, we avoid collision where two robots use the same edge in opposite directions. This can always be done since there are strictly more than 2​k2k vertices of each type that does not include the vertex identity. Recall that if such a collision happens due to types that contain vertex identities, then the third of the above-described checks fails.

  • •

    If after the iith move is performed for each movement, a robot rr is moved to a vertex vv of some type tt that is occupied by another robot r′r^{\prime}, then we moved robot rr to the “wrong” vertex type tt.

    Since the second of the above-described checks did not fail, there must be another vertex v′v^{\prime} of type tt that is not occupied by any robot after the iith move. Furthermore, since the last of the above-described checks did not fail, we know that r′r^{\prime} was already on vv in the previous step.

    We introduce an intermediate step (between steps i−1i-1 and ii) in which we move robot r′r^{\prime} from vv to v′v^{\prime}.

By construction, the above described movements are collision-free. Furthermore, the resulting movement plan as length at most 2​c2c since for every move in the type vectors we add at most one additional move in the second of the above-described steps of the construction.

To ensure that the end-configuration is connected, we have to move the main robots to the vertices specified by the embedding ϕ\phi of the tree TT on the main robots. By construction, we have that ℳ\mathcal{M} moves each main robot to a vertex that has the same type as its target vertex in the embedding ϕ\phi. Note that all vertices of the same type are in the same clique. In a final step, we move each main robot onto their target vertex using at most three moves.

Assume that there is a main robot rr which is not on its target vertex vv. If the target vertex vv is free, we can move rr to that vertex with one additional move. If the target vertex vv is occupied by some robot r′r^{\prime}, then we pick another vertex v′v^{\prime} of the same type that is not occupied by a main robot. Note that since there are at least 2​k+c+22k+c+2 vertices of each type (that does not include the vertex identity), such a vertex exits. If v′v^{\prime} is free, then we move the robot r′r^{\prime} to v′v^{\prime}, and afterwards we move rr to vv. If v′v^{\prime} is occupied by an obnoxious robot r′′r^{\prime\prime}, we perform a cyclic move. Let v′′v^{\prime\prime} be the current position of rr. We simultaneously move robot rr to vv, robot r′r^{\prime} to v′v^{\prime}, and robot r′′r^{\prime\prime} to v′′v^{\prime\prime}. All described movements are clearly collision-free, contain at most three moves, and reduce the number of main robots that are not on their target vertex by one. Hence, by iterating this procedure, we can move all main robots to their respective target vertices in a collision-free manner by using at most three additional moves per main robot.

Now we are ready to prove Theorem 9.

Proof of Theorem 9.

It is straightforward to check that the described guesses create f⁡(k+c)⋅nO⁡(1)f(k+c)\cdot n^{O(1)} cases, the described checks can be performed in f⁡(k+c)⋅nO⁡(1)f(k+c)\cdot n^{O(1)} time, and the movement plan can be constructed in f⁡(k+c)⋅nO⁡(1)f(k+c)\cdot n^{O(1)} time.

As argued during the description, the algorithm clearly produces a collision-free movement plan such that the end-configuration of the main robots is connected.

Now assume there is an optimal solution ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} of length cc to the Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity instance. Then there is a guess such that the each type vector corresponds to one movement in ℳ⋆\mathcal{M}^{\star} and the tree TT corresponds to a spanning tree in the subgraph of the main robots in their end-configuration. As argued, the movement plan constructed by the algorithm then has length at most 2​c+3​k2c+3k. It follows that we compute a 2-approximation with an additional additive error of 3​k3k. ∎

8 Conclusion

To the best of our knowledge, we give the first computational results for the problems Collision-Free Movement to Π\Pi and Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity. We leave several open questions. We believe that the following are of particular interest.

  • •

    Is Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by cc if the input graph is planar?

  • •

    Is Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized by k+ck+c if the input graph is a unit disk graph?

It would also be interesting to identify graph classes on which Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity becomes solvable in polynomial time.

  • •

    Is Collision-Free Movement to Connectivity solvable in polynomial time if the input graph is a tree?

It is also natural to consider other parameters, such as e.g. the number of obnoxious robots or structural parameters of the input graph such as the treewidth.

Apart from these relatively specific questions, our work opens several natural future work directions. Instead of minimizing the total movement (energy) one could ask to minimize the makespan of the movement plan instead. There are also many other natural graph properties that one could focus on, for example one could require that the target formation admits a perfect matching among the main robots (for an even number of robots). Notably, for two robots this coincides with connectivity, and hence some of our hardness results transfer.
